verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:68
verses.text: But even the Lord concealed the truth, when He said to the disciples, not yet strong enough, "I have many things to say unto you, but ye cannot bear them now:" and the Apostle Paul when he said, "I could not speak unto you as unto spiritual, but as unto carnal".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:69
verses.text: Whence it is clear that it is not blamable, sometimes not to speak what is true.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:70
verses.text: But to say what is false is not found to have been allowed to the perfect.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:71
verses.text: "The man of blood, and the crafty man, the Lord will abominate".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:72
verses.text: What he said above, "Thou hast hated all that work iniquity, Thou wilt destroy all that speak a lie," may well seem to be repeated here: so that one may refer "the man of blood" to "the worker of iniquity," and "the crafty man" to the "lie".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:73
verses.text: For it is craft, when one thing is done, another pretended.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:74
verses.text: He used an apt word too, when he  said, "will abominate".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:75
verses.text: For the disinherited are usually called abominated.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:76
verses.text: Now this Psalm is, "for her who receiveth the inheritance;" and she adds the exulting joy of her hope, in saying, "But I, in the multitude of Thy mercy, will enter into Thine house".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:77
verses.text: "In the multitude of mercy:" perhaps he means in the multitude of perfected and blessed men, of whom that city shall consist, of which the Church is now in travail, and is bearing few by few.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:78
verses.text: Now that many men regenerated and perfected, are rightly called the multitude of God's mercy, who can deny; when it is most truly said, "What is man that Thou art mindful of him, or the son of man that Thou visitest him? I will enter into Thine house:" as a stone into a building, I suppose, is the meaning.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:79
verses.text: For what else is the house of God than the Temple of God, of which it is said, "for the temple of God is holy, which temple ye are"? Of which building He is the cornerstone, whom the Power and Wisdom of God coeternal with the Father assumed.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:80
verses.text: "I will worship at Thy holy temple, in Thy fear".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:81
verses.text: "At the temple," we understand as, "near" the temple.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:82
verses.text: For he does not say, I will worship "in" Thy holy temple; but, "I will worship at Thy holy temple".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:83
verses.text: It must be understood too to be spoken not of perfection, but of progress toward perfection: so that the words, "I will enter into Thine house," should signify perfection.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:84
verses.text: But that this may come to a happy issue, "I will" first, he says, "worship at Thy holy temple".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:85
verses.text: And perhaps on this account he added, "in Thy fear;" which is a great defence to those that are advancing toward salvation.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:86
verses.text: But when any one shall have arrived there, in him comes to pass that which is written, "perfect love casteth out fear".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:87
verses.text: For they do not fear Him who is now their friend, to whom it is said, "henceforth I will not call you servants, but friends," when they have been brought through to that which was promised.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:88
verses.text: "O Lord, lead me forth in Thy justice because of mine enemies".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:89
verses.text: He has here sufficiently plainly declared that he is on his onward road, that is, in progress toward perfection, not yet in perfection itself, when he desires eagerly that he may be led forth.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:90
verses.text: But, "in Thy justice," not in that which seems so to men.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:91
verses.text: For to return evil for evil seems justice: but it is not His justice of whom it is said, "He maketh His sun to rise on the good and on the evil:" for even when God punishes sinners, He does not inflict His evil on them, but leaves them to their own evil.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:92
verses.text: "Behold," the Psalmist says, "he travailed with injustice, he hath conceived toil, and brought forth iniquity: he hath opened a ditch, and digged it, and hath fallen into the pit which he wrought: his pains shall be turned on his own head, and his iniquity shall descend on his own pate".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:93
verses.text: When then God punishes, He punishes as a judge those that transgress the law, not by bringing evil upon them from Himself, but driving them on to that which they have chosen, to fill up the sum of their misery.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:94
verses.text: But man, when he returns evil for evil, does it with an evil will: and on this account is himself first evil, when he would punish evil.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:95
verses.text: "Direct in Thy sight my way".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:96
verses.text: Nothing is clearer, than that he here sets forth that time, in which he is journeying onward.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:97
verses.text: For this is a way which is traversed not in any regions of the earth, but in the affections of the heart.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:98
verses.text: "In Thy sight," he says, "direct my way:" that is, where no man sees; who are not to be trusted in their praise or blame.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:99
verses.text: For they can in no wise judge of another man's conscience, wherein the way toward God is traversed.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:100
verses.text: Hence it is added, "for truth is not in their mouth".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:101
verses.text: To whose judgment of course then there is no trusting, and therefore must we fly within to conscience, and the sight of God.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:102
verses.text: "Their heart is vain".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:103
verses.text: How then can truth be in their mouth, whose heart is deceived by sin, and the punishment of sin? Whence men are called back by that voice, "Wherefore do ye love vanity, and seek a lie?".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:104
verses.text: "Their throat is an open sepulchre".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:105
verses.text: It may be referred to signify gluttony, for the sake of which men very often lie by flattery.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:106
verses.text: And admirably has he said, "an open sepulchre:" for this gluttony is ever gaping with open mouth, not as sepulchres, which, on the reception of corpses, are closed up.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:107
verses.text: This also may be understood hereby, that with lying and blind flattery men draw to themselves those whom they entice to sin; and as it were devour them, when they turn them to their own way of living.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:108
verses.text: And when this happens to them, since by sin they die, those by whom they are led along, are rightly called open sepulchres: for themselves too are in a manner lifeless, being destitute of the life of truth; and they take in to themselves dead men, whom having slain by lying words and a vain heart, they turn unto themselves.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:109
verses.text: "With their own tongues they dealt craftily:" that is, with evil tongues.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:110
verses.text: For this seems to be signified, when he says "their own".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:111
verses.text: For the evil have evil tongues, that is, they speak evil, when they speak craftily.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:112
verses.text: To whom the Lord saith, "How can ye, being evil, speak good things?".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:113
verses.text: "Judge them, O God: let them fall from their own thoughts".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:114
verses.text: It is a prophecy, not a curse.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:115
verses.text: For he does not wish that it should come to pass; but he perceives what will come to pass.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:116
verses.text: For this happens to them, not because he appears to have wished for it, but because they are such as to deserve that it should happen.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:117
verses.text: For so also what he says afterwards, "Let all that hope in Thee rejoice," he says by way of prophecy; since he perceives that they will rejoice.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:118
verses.text: Likewise is it said prophetically, "Stir up Thy strength, and come:" for he saw that He would come.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:119
verses.text: Although the words, "Let them fall from their own thoughts," may be taken thus also, that it may rather be believed to be a wish for their good by the Psalmist, whilst they fall from their evil thoughts, that is, that they may no more think evil.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:120
verses.text: But what follows, "drive them out," forbids this interpretation.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:121
verses.text: For it can in no wise be taken in a favourable sense, that one is driven out by God.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:122
verses.text: Wherefore it is understood to be said prophetically, and not of ill will; when this is said, which must necessarily happen to such as chose to persevere in those sins, which have been mentioned.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:123
verses.text: "Let them," therefore, "fall from their own thoughts," is, let them fall by their self-accusing thoughts, "their own conscience also bearing witness," as the Apostle says, "and their thoughts accusing or excusing, in the revelation of the just judgment of God".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:124
verses.text: "According to the multitude of their ungodlinesses drive them out:" that is, drive them out far away.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:125
verses.text: For this is "according to the multitude of their ungodlinesses," that they should be driven out far away.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:126
verses.text: The ungodly then are driven out from that inheritance, which is possessed by knowing and seeing God: as diseased eyes are driven out from the shining of the light, when what is gladness to others is pain to them.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:127
verses.text: Therefore these shall not stand in the morning, and see.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:128
verses.text: And that expression is as great a punishment, as that which is said, "But for me it is good to cleave to the Lord," is a great reward.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:129
verses.text: To this punishment is opposed, "Enter thou into the joy of Thy Lord;" for similar to this expulsion is, "Cast him into outer darkness".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:130
verses.text: "Since they have embittered Thee, O Lord: I am," saith He, "the Bread which came down from heaven;" again, "Labour for the meat which wasteth not;" again, "Taste and see that the Lord is sweet".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:131
verses.text: But to sinners the bread of truth is bitter.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:132
verses.text: Whence they hate the mouth of him that speaketh the truth.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:133
verses.text: These then have embittered God, who by sin have fallen into such a state of sickliness, that the food of truth, in which healthy souls delight, as if it were bitter as gall, they cannot bear.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:134
verses.text: "And let all rejoice that hope in Thee;" those of course to whose taste the Lord is sweet.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:135
verses.text: "They will exult for evermore, and Thou wilt dwell in them".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:136
verses.text: This will be the exultation for evermore, when the just become the Temple of God, and He, their Indweller, will be their joy.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:137
verses.text: "And all that love Thy name shall glory in Thee:" as when what they love is present for them to enjoy.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:138
verses.text: And well is  it said, "in Thee," as if in possession of the inheritance, of which the title of the Psalm speaks: when they too are His inheritance, which is intimated by, "Thou wilt dwell in them".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:139
verses.text: From which good they are kept back, whom God, according to the multitude of their ungodlinesses, driveth out.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:140
verses.text: "For Thou wilt bless the just man".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:141
verses.text: This is blessing, to glory in God, and to be inhabited by God.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:142
verses.text: Such sanctification is given to the just.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:143
verses.text: But that they may be justified, a calling goes before: which is not of merit, but of the grace of God.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:144
verses.text: "For all have sinned, and want the glory of God".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:145
verses.text: "For whom He called, them He also justified; and whom He justified, them He also glorified".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:146
verses.text: Since then calling is not of our merit, but of the goodness and mercy of God, he went on to say, "O Lord, as with the shield of Thy good will Thou hast crowned us".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:147
verses.text: For God's good will goes before our good will, to call sinners to repentance.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:148
verses.text: And these are the arms whereby the enemy is overcome, against whom it is said, "Who will bring accusation against God's elect?" Again, "if God be for us, who can be against us? Who spared not His Only Son, but delivered Him up for us all".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:149
verses.text: "For if, when we were enemies, Christ died for us; much more being reconciled shall we be saved from wrath through Him".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:150
verses.text: This is that unconquerable shield, whereby the enemy is driven back, when he suggests despair of our salvation through the multitude of tribulations and temptations.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:151
verses.text: The whole contents of the Psalm, then, are a prayer that she may be heard, from the words, "hear my words, O Lord," unto, "my King, and my God".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:152
verses.text: Then follows a view of those things which hinder the sight of God, that is, a knowledge that she is heard, from the words, "because I shall pray unto Thee, O Lord, in the morning Thou wilt hear my voice," unto, "the man of blood and the crafty man the Lord will abominate".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:153
verses.text: Thirdly, she hopes that she, who is to be the house of God, even now begins to draw near to Him in fear, before that perfection which casteth out fear, from the words, "but I in the multitude of Thy mercy," unto, "I will worship at Thy holy temple in Thy fear".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:154
verses.text: Fourthly, as she is progressing and advancing amongst those very things which she feels to hinder her, she prays that she may be assisted within, where no man seeth, lest she be turned aside by evil tongues, for the words, "O Lord, lead me forth in Thy justice because of my enemies," unto, "with their tongues they dealt craftily".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 5:155
verses.text: Fifthly, is a prophecy of what punishment awaits the ungodly, when the just man shall scarcely be saved; and of what reward the just shall obtain, who, when they were called, came, and bore all things manfully, till they were brought to the end, from the words, "judge them, O God," unto the end of the Psalm.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:1
verses.text: Psalm VI.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:2
verses.text: To the end, in the hymns of the eighth, a psalm to David.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:3
verses.text: "Of the eighth," seems here obscure.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:4
verses.text: For the rest of this title is more clear.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:5
verses.text: Now it has seemed to some to intimate the day of judgment, that is, the time of the coming of our Lord, when He will come to judge the quick and dead.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:6
verses.text: Which coming, it is believed, is to be, after reckoning the years from Adam, seven thousand years: so as that seven thousand years should pass as seven days, and afterwards that time arrive as it were the eighth day.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:7
verses.text: But since it has been said by the Lord, "It is not yours to know the times, which the Father hath put in His own power:" and, "But of the day and that hour knoweth no man, no, neither angel, nor Power, neither the Son, but the Father alone:" and again, that which is written, "that the day of the Lord cometh as a thief," shows clearly enough that no man should arrogate to himself the knowledge of that time, by any computation of years.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:8
verses.text: For if that day is to come after seven thousand years, every man could learn its advent by reckoning the years.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:9
verses.text: What comes then of the Son's even not knowing this? Which of course is said with this meaning, that men do not learn this by the Son, not that He by Himself doth not know it: according to that form of speech, "the Lord your God trieth you that He may know;" that is, that He may make you know: and, "arise, O Lord;" that is, make us arise.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:10
verses.text: When therefore the Son is thus said not to know this day; not because He knoweth it not, but because He causeth those to know it not, for whom it is not expedient to know it, that is, He doth not show it to them; what does that strange presumption mean, which, by a reckoning up of years, expects the day of the Lord as most certain after seven thousand years?.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:11
verses.text: Be we then willingly ignorant of that which the Lord would not have us know: and let us inquire what this title, "of the eighth," means.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:12
verses.text: The day of judgment may indeed, even without any rash computation of years, be understood by the eighth, for that immediately after the end of this world, life eternal being attained, the souls of the righteous will not then be subject unto times: and, since all times have their revolution in a repetition of those seven days, that peradventure is called the eighth day, which will not have this variety.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:13
verses.text: There is another reason, which may be here not unreasonably accepted, why the judgment should be called the eighth, because it will take place after two generations, one relating to the body, the other to the soul.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:14
verses.text: For from Adam unto Moses the human race lived of the body, that is, according to the flesh: which is called the outward and the old man, and to which the Old Testament was given, that it might prefigure the spiritual things to come by operations, albeit religious, yet carnal.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:15
verses.text: Through this entire season, when men lived according to the body, "death reigned," as the Apostle saith, "even over those that had not sinned".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:16
verses.text: Now it reigned "after the similitude of Adam's transgression," as the same Apostle saith; for it must be taken of the period up to Moses, up to which time the works of the law, that is, those sacraments of carnal observance, held even those bound, for the sake of a certain mystery, who were subject to the One God.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:17
verses.text: But from the coming of the Lord, from whom there was a transition from the circumcision of the flesh to the circumcision of the heart, the call was made, that man should live according to the soul, that is, according to the inner man, who is also called the "new man" by reason of the new birth and the renewing of spiritual conversation.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:18
verses.text: Now it is plain that the number four has relation to the body, from the four well known elements of which it consists, and the four qualities of dry, humid, warm, cold.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:19
verses.text: Hence too it is administered by four seasons, spring, summer, autumn, winter.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:20
verses.text: All this is very well known.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:21
verses.text: For of the number four relating to the body we have treated elsewhere somewhat subtilly, but obscurely: which must be avoided in this discourse, which we would have accommodated to the unlearned.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:22
verses.text: But that the number three has relation to the mind may be understood from this, that we are commanded to love God after a threefold manner, with the whole heart, with the whole soul, with the whole mind: of each of which severally we must treat, not in the Psalms, but in the Gospels: for the present, for proof of the relation of the number three to the mind, I think what has been said enough.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:23
verses.text: Those numbers then of the body which have relation to the old man and the Old Testament, being past and gone, the numbers too of the soul, which have relation to the new man and the New Testament, being past and gone, a septenary so to say being passed; because everything is done in time, four having been distributed to the body, three to the mind; the eighth will come, the day of judgment: which assigning to deserts their due, will transfer at once the saint, not to temporal works, but to eternal life; but will condemn the ungodly to eternal punishment.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:24
verses.text: In fear of which condemnation the Church prays in this Psalm, and says, "Reprove me not, O Lord, in Thine anger".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:25
verses.text: The Apostle too mentions the anger of the judgment; "Thou treasurest up unto thyself," he says, "anger against the day of the anger of the just judgment of God".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:26
verses.text: In which he would not be reproved, whosoever longs to be healed in this life.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:27
verses.text: "Nor in Thy rage chasten me".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:28
verses.text: "Chasten," seems rather too mild a word; for it availeth toward amendment.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:29
verses.text: For for him who is reproved, that is, accused, it is to be feared lest his end be condemnation.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:30
verses.text: But since "rage" seems to be more than "anger," it may be a difficulty, why that which is milder, namely, chastening, is joined to that which is more severe, namely, rage.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:31
verses.text: But I suppose that one and the same thing is signified by the two words.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:32
verses.text: For in the Greek θυμὸς, which is in the first verse, means the same as ὀργὴ, which is in the second verse But when the Latins themselves too wished to use two distinct words, they looked out for what was akin to "anger," and "rage" was used.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:33
verses.text: Hence copies vary.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:34
verses.text: For in some "anger" is found first, and then "rage:" in others, for "rage," "indignation" or "choler" is used.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:35
verses.text: But whatever the reading, it is an emotion of the soul urging to the infliction of punishment.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:36
verses.text: Yet this emotion must not be attributed to God, as if to a soul, of whom it is said, "but Thou, O Lord of power, judgest with tranquillity".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:37
verses.text: Now that which is tranquil, is not disturbed.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:38
verses.text: Disturbance then does not attach to God as judge: but what is done by His ministers, in that it is done by His laws, is called His anger.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:39
verses.text: In which anger, the soul, which now prays, would not only not be reproved, but not even chastened, that is, amended or instructed.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:40
verses.text: For in the Greek it is, παιδεύσῃς, that is, instruct.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:41
verses.text: Now in the day of judgment all are "reproved" that hold not the foundation, which is Christ.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:42
verses.text: But they are amended, that is, purged, who "upon this foundation build wood, hay, stubble.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:43
verses.text: For they shall suffer loss, but shall be saved, as by fire".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:44
verses.text: What then does he pray, who would not be either reproved or amended in the anger of the Lord? what else but that he may be healed? For where sound health is, neither death is to be dreaded, nor the physician's hand with caustics or the knife.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:45
verses.text: He proceeds accordingly to say, "Pity me, O Lord, for I am weak: heal me, O Lord, for my bones are troubled" , that is, the support of my soul, or strength: for this is the meaning of "bones".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:46
verses.text: The soul therefore says, that her strength is troubled, when she speaks of bones.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:47
verses.text: For it is not to be supposed, that the soul has bones, such as we see in the body.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:48
verses.text: Wherefore, what follows tends to explain it, "and my soul is troubled exceedingly" , lest because he mentioned bones, they should be understood as of the body.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:49
verses.text: "And Thou, O Lord, how long?" Who does not see represented here a soul struggling with her diseases; but long kept back by the physician, that she may be convinced what evils she has plunged herself into through sin? For what is easily healed, is not much avoided: but from the difficulty of the healing, there will be the more careful keeping of recovered health.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:50
verses.text: God then, to whom it is said, "And Thou, O Lord, how long?" must not be deemed as if cruel: but as a kind convincer of the soul, what evil she hath procured for herself.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:51
verses.text: For this soul does not yet pray so perfectly, as that it can be said to her, "Whilst thou art yet speaking I will say, Behold, here I am".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:52
verses.text: That she may at the same time also come to know, if they who do turn meet with so great difficulty, how great punishment is prepared for the ungodly, who will not turn to God: as it is written in another place, "If the righteous scarcely be saved, where shall the sinner and ungodly appear?".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:53
verses.text: "Turn, O Lord, and deliver my soul".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:54
verses.text: Turning herself she prays that God too would turn to her: as it is said, "Turn ye unto Me, and I will turn unto you, saith the Lord".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:55
verses.text: Or is it to be understood according to that way of speaking, "Turn, O Lord," that is make me turn, since the soul in this her turning feels difficulty and toil? For our perfected turning findeth God ready, as says the Prophet, "We shall find Him ready as the dawn".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:56
verses.text: Since it was not His absence who is everywhere present, but our turning away that made us lose Him; "He was in this world," it is said, "and the world was made by Him, and the world knew Him not".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:57
verses.text: If, then, He was in this world, and the world knew Him not, our impurity doth not endure the sight of Him.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:58
verses.text: But whilst we are turning ourselves, that is, by changing our old life are fashioning our spirit; we feel it hard and toilsome to be wrested back from the darkness of earthly lusts, to the serene and quiet and tranquillity of the divine light.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:59
verses.text: And in such difficulty we say, "Turn, O Lord," that is, help us, that that turning may be perfected in us, which findeth Thee ready, and offering Thyself for the fruition of them that love Thee.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:60
verses.text: And hence after he said, "Turn, O Lord," he added, "and deliver my soul:" cleaving as it were to the entanglements of this world, and suffering, in the very act of turning, from the thorns, as it were, of rending and tearing desires.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:61
verses.text: "Make me whole," he says, "for Thy pity's sake".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:62
verses.text: He knows that it is not of his own merits that he is healed: for to him sinning, and transgressing a given command, was just condemnation due.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:63
verses.text: Heal me therefore, he says, not for my merit's sake, but for Thy pity's sake.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:64
verses.text: "For in death there is no one that is mindful of Thee".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:65
verses.text: He knows too that now is the time for turning unto God: for when this life shall have passed away, there remaineth but a retribution of our deserts "But in hell who shall confess to Thee?" That rich man, of whom the Lord speaks, who saw Lazarus in rest, but bewailed himself in torments, confessed in hell, yea so as to wish even to have his brethren warned, that they might keep themselves from sin, because of the punishment which is not believed to be in hell.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:66
verses.text: Although therefore to no purpose, yet he confessed that those torments had deservedly lighted upon him; since he even wished his brethren to be instructed, lest they should fall into the same.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:67
verses.text: What then is, "But in hell who will confess to Thee?" Is hell to be understood as that place, whither the ungodly will be cast down after the judgment, when by reason of that deeper darkness they will no more see any light of God, to whom they may confess aught? For as yet that rich man by raising his eyes, although a vast gulf lay between, could still see Lazarus established in rest: by comparing himself with whom, he was driven to a confession of his own deserts.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:68
verses.text: It may be understood also, as if the Psalmist calls sin, that is committed in contempt of God's law, death: so as that we should give the name of death to the sting of death, because it procures death.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:69
verses.text: "For the sting of death is sin".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:70
verses.text: In which death this is to be unmindful of God, to despise His law and commandments: so that by hell the Psalmist would mean that blindness of soul which overtakes and enwraps the sinner, that is, the dying.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:71
verses.text: "As they did not think good," the Apostle says, "to retain God in" their "knowledge, God gave them over to a reprobate mind".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:72
verses.text: From this death, and this hell, the soul earnestly prays that she may be kept safe, whilst she strives to turn to God, and feels her difficulties.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:73
verses.text: Wherefore he goes on to say, "I have laboured in my groaning".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:74
verses.text: And as if this availed but little, he adds, "I will wash each night my couch".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:75
verses.text: That is here called a couch, where the sick and weak soul rests, that is, in bodily gratification and in every worldly pleasure.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:76
verses.text: Which pleasure, whoso endeavours to withdraw himself from it, washes with tears.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:77
verses.text: For he sees that he already condemns carnal lusts; and yet his weakness is held by the pleasure, and willingly lies down therein, from whence none but the soul that is made whole can rise.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:78
verses.text: As for what he says, "each night," he would perhaps have it taken thus: that he who, ready in spirit, perceives some light of truth, and yet, through weakness of the flesh, rests sometime in the pleasure of this world, is compelled to suffer as it were days and nights in an alternation of feeling: as when he says, "With the mind I serve the law of God," he feels as it were day; again when he says, "but with the flesh the law of sin," he declines into night: until all night passeth away, and that one day comes, of which it is said, "In the morning I will stand by Thee, and will see".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:79
verses.text: For then he will stand, but now he lies down, when he is on his couch; which he will wash each night, that with so great abundance of tears he may obtain the most assured remedy from the mercy of God.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:80
verses.text: "I will drench my bed with tears".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:81
verses.text: It is a repetition For when he says, "with tears," he shows with what meaning he said above, "I will wash".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:82
verses.text: For we take "bed" here to be the same as "couch" above.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:83
verses.text: Although, "I will drench," is something more than, "I will wash:" since anything may be washed superficially, but drenching penetrates to the more inward parts; which here signifies weeping to the very bottom of the heart.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:84
verses.text: Now the variety of tenses which he uses; the past, when he said, "I have laboured in my groaning;" and the future, when he said, "I will wash each night my couch;" the future again, "I will drench my bed with tears;" this shows what every man ought to say to himself, when he labours in groaning to no purpose.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:85
verses.text: As if he should say, It hath not profited when I have done this, therefore I will do the other.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:86
verses.text: "Mine eye is disordered by anger" : is it by his own, or God's anger, in which he maketh petition that he might not be reproved, or chastened? But if anger in that place intimate the day of judgment, how can it be understood now? Is it a beginning of it, that men here suffer pains and torments, and above all the loss of the understanding of the truth; as I have already quoted that which is said, "God gave them over to a reprobate mind"? For such is the blindness of the mind.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:87
verses.text: Whosoever is given over thereunto, is shut out from the interior light of God: but not wholly as yet, whilst he is in this life.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:88
verses.text: For there is "outer darkness," which is understood to belong rather to the day of judgment; that he should rather be wholly without God, whosoever whilst there is time refuses correction.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:89
verses.text: Now to be wholly without God, what else is it, but to be in extreme blindness? If indeed God "dwell in inaccessible light," whereinto they enter, to whom it is said, "Enter thou into the joy of thy Lord".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:90
verses.text: It is then the beginning of this anger, which in this life every sinner suffers.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:91
verses.text: In fear therefore of the day of judgment, he is in trial and grief; lest he be brought to that, the disastrous commencement of which he experiences now.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:92
verses.text: And therefore he did not say, mine eye is extinguished, but, "mine eye is disordered by anger".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:93
verses.text: But if he mean that his eye is disordered by his own anger, there is no wonder either in this.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:94
verses.text: For hence perhaps it is said, "Let not the sun go down upon your wrath;" because the mind, which, from her own disorder, is not permitted to see God, supposes that the inner sun, that is, the wisdom of God, suffers as it were a setting in her.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:95
verses.text: "I have grown old in all mine enemies".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:96
verses.text: He had only spoken of anger (if it were yet of his own anger that he spoke): but thinking on his other vices, he found that he was entrenched by them all.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:97
verses.text: Which vices, as they belong to the old life and the old man, which we must put off, that we may put on the new man, it is well said, "I have grown old".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:98
verses.text: But "in all mine enemies," he means, either amidst these vices, or amidst men who will not be converted to God.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:99
verses.text: For these, even if they know them not, even if they bear with them, even if they use the same tables and houses and cities, with no strife arising between them, and in frequent converse together with seeming concord: notwithstanding, by the contrariety of their aims, they are enemies to those who turn unto God.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:100
verses.text: For seeing that the one love and desire this world, the others wish to be freed from this world, who sees not that the first are enemies to the last? For if they can, they draw the others into punishment with them.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:101
verses.text: And it is a great grace, to be conversant daily with their words, and not to depart from the way of God's commandments.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:102
verses.text: For often the mind which is striving to go on to God-ward, being rudely handled in the very road, is alarmed; and generally fulfils not its good intent, lest it should offend those with whom it lives, who love and follow after other perishable and transient goods.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:103
verses.text: From such every one that is whole is separated, not in space, but in soul.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:104
verses.text: For the body is contained in space, but the soul's space is her affection.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:105
verses.text: Wherefore after the labour, and groaning, and very frequent showers of tears, since that cannot be ineffectual, which is asked so earnestly of Him, who is the Fountain of all mercies, and it is most truly said, "the Lord is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart:" after difficulties so great, the pious soul, by which we may also understand the Church, intimating that she has been heard, see what she adds: "Depart from me, all ye that work iniquity; for the Lord hath heard the voice of my weeping".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:106
verses.text: It is either spoken prophetically, since they will depart, that is, the ungodly will be separated from the righteous, when the day of judgment arrives, or, for this time present.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:107
verses.text: For although both are equally found in the same assemblies, yet on the open floor the wheat is already separated from the chaff, though it be hid among the chaff.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:108
verses.text: They can therefore be associated together, but cannot be carried away by the wind together.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:109
verses.text: "For the Lord hath heard the voice of my weeping; The Lord hath heard my supplication; the Lord hath received my prayer".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:110
verses.text: The frequent repetition of the same sentiments shows not, so to say, the necessities of the narrator, but the warm feeling of his joy.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:111
verses.text: For they that rejoice are wont so to speak, as that it is not enough for them to declare once for all the object of their joy.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:112
verses.text: This is the fruit of that groaning in which there is labour, and those tears with which the couch is washed, and bed drenched: for, "he that sows in tears, shall reap in joy:"  and, "blessed are they that mourn, for they shall be comforted".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:113
verses.text: "Let all mine enemies be ashamed and vexed".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:114
verses.text: He said above, "depart from me all ye:" which can take place, as it has been explained, even in this life: but as to what he says, "let them be ashamed and vexed," I do not see how it can happen, save on that day when the rewards of the righteous and the punishments of the sinners shall be made manifest.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:115
verses.text: For at present so far are the ungodly from being ashamed, that they do not cease to insult us.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:116
verses.text: And for the most part their mockings are of such avail, that they make the weak to be ashamed of the name of Christ.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:117
verses.text: Hence it is said, "Whosoever shall be ashamed of Me before men, of him will I be ashamed before My Father".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:118
verses.text: But now whosoever would fulfil those sublime commands, to disperse, to give to the poor, that his righteousness may endure for ever; and selling all his earthly goods, and spending them on the needy, would follow Christ, saying, "We brought nothing into this world, and truly we can carry nothing out; having food and raiment, let us be therewith content;" incurs the profane raillery of those men, and by those who will not be made whole, is called mad; and often to avoid being so called by desperate men, he fears to do, and puts off that, which the most faithful and powerful of all physicians hath ordered.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:119
verses.text: It is not then at present that these can be ashamed, by whom we have to wish that we be not made ashamed, and so be either called back from our proposed journey, or hindered, or delayed.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:120
verses.text: But the time will come when they shall be ashamed, saying as it is written, "These are they whom we had sometimes in derision, and a parable of reproach: we fools counted their life madness, and their end to be without honour: how are they numbered among the children of God, and their lot is among the saints? Therefore have we erred from the way of truth, and the light of righteousness hath not shined into us, nor the sun risen upon us: we have been filled with the way of wickedness and destruction, and have walked through rugged deserts, but the way of the Lord we have not known.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:121
verses.text: What hath pride profited us, or what hath the vaunting of riches brought us? All those things are passed away like a shadow".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:122
verses.text: But as to what he says, "Let them be turned and confounded," who would not judge it to be a most righteous punishment, that they should have a turning unto confusion, who would not have one unto salvation? After this he added, "exceeding quickly".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:123
verses.text: For when the day of judgment shall have begun to be no longer looked for, when they shall have said, "Peace, then shall sudden destruction come upon them".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:124
verses.text: Now whensoever it come, that comes very quickly, of whose coming we give up all expectation; and nothing makes the length of this life be felt but the hope of living.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:125
verses.text: For nothing seems more quick, than all that has already passed in it.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:126
verses.text: When then the day of judgment shall come, then will sinners feel how that all the life which passeth away is not long.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:127
verses.text: Nor will that any way possibly seem to them to have come tardily, which shall have come without their desiring, or rather without their believing.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:128
verses.text: Although it can too be taken in this place thus, that inasmuch as God has heard, so to say, her groans, and her long and frequent tears, she may be understood to be freed from her sins, and to have tamed every disordered impulse of carnal affection: as she saith, "Depart from me, all ye that work iniquity, for the Lord hath heard the voice of my weeping:" and when she has had this happy issue, it is no marvel if she be already so perfect as to pray for her enemies.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:129
verses.text: The words then, "Let all mine enemies be ashamed, and vexed," may have this meaning; that they should repent of their sins, which cannot be effected without confusion and vexation.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 6:130
verses.text: There is then nothing to hinder us from taking what follows too in this sense, "let them be turned and ashamed," that is, let them be turned to God, and be ashamed that they sometime gloried in the former darkness of their sins; as the Apostle says, "For what glory had ye sometime in those things of which ye are now ashamed?" But as to what he added, "exceeding quickly," it must be referred either to the warm affection of her wish, or to the power of Christ; who converteth to the faith of the Gospel in such quick time the nations, which in their idols' cause did persecute the Church.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:1
verses.text: Psalm VII.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:2
verses.text: A psalm to David himself, which he sung to the Lord, for the words of Chusi, son of Jemini.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:3
verses.text: Now the story which gave occasion to this prophecy may be easily recognised in the second book of Kings For there Chusi, the friend of king David, went over to the side of Abessalon, his son, who was carrying on war against his father, for the purpose of discovering and reporting the designs which he was taking against his father, at the instigation of Achitophel, who had revolted from David's friendship, and was instructing by his counsel, to the best of his power, the son against the father.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:4
verses.text: But since it is not the story itself which is to be the subject of consideration in this Psalm, from which the prophet hath taken a veil of mysteries, if we have passed over to Christ, let the veil be taken away And first let us inquire into the signification of the very names, what it means.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:5
verses.text: For there have not been wanting interpreters, who investigating these same words, not carnally according to the letter, but spiritually, declare to us that Chusi should be interpreted silence; and Gemini, right-handed; Achitophel, brother's ruin.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:6
verses.text: Among which interpretations, Judas, that traitor, again meets us, that Abessalon should bear his image, according to that interpretation of it as a father's peace; in that his father was full of thoughts of peace toward him: although he in his guile had war in his heart, as was treated of in the third Psalm.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:7
verses.text: Now as we find in the Gospels that the disciples of our Lord Jesus Christ are called sons, so in the same Gospels we find they are called brethren also.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:8
verses.text: For the Lord on the resurrection saith, "Go and say to My brethren".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:9
verses.text: And the Apostle calls Him "the first begotten among many brethren".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:10
verses.text: The ruin then of that disciple, who betrayed Him, is rightly understood to be a brother's ruin, which we said is the interpretation of Achitophel.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:11
verses.text: Now as to Chusi, from the interpretation of silence, it is rightly understood that our Lord contended against that guile in silence, that is, in that most deep secret, whereby "blindness happened in part to Israel," when they were persecuting the Lord, that the fulness of the Gentiles might enter in, and "so all Israel might be saved".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:12
verses.text: When the Apostle came to this profound secret and deep silence, he exclaimed, as if struck with a kind of awe of its very depth, "O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! how unsearchable are His judgments, and His ways past finding out! For who hath known the wind of the Lord, or who hath been His counsellor?"  Thus that great silence he does not so much discover by explanation, as he sets forth its greatness in admiration.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:13
verses.text: In this silence the Lord, hiding the sacrament of His adorable passion, turns the brother's voluntary ruin, that is, His betrayer's impious wickedness, into the order of His mercy and providence: that what he with perverse mind wrought for one Man's destruction, He might by providential overruling dispose for all men's sa lvation.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:14
verses.text: The perfect soul then, which is already worthy to know the secret of God, sings a Psalm unto the Lord, she sings "for the words of Chusi," because she has attained to know the words of that silence: for among unbelievers and persecutors there is that silence and secret.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:15
verses.text: But among His own, to whom it is said, "Now I call you no more servants; for the servant knoweth not what his lord doeth; but I have called you friends, for all things that I have heard of My Father I have made known unto you:  among His friends, I say, there is not the silence, but the words of the silence, that is, the meaning of that silence set forth and manifested.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:16
verses.text: Which silence, that is, Chusi, is called the son of Gemini, that is, righthanded.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:17
verses.text: For what was done for the Saints was not to be hidden from them.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:18
verses.text: And yet He saith, "Let not the left hand know what the right hand doeth".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:19
verses.text: The perfect soul then, to which that secret has been made known, sings in prophecy "for the words of Chusi," that is, for the knowledge of that same secret.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:20
verses.text: Which secret God at her right hand, that is, favourable and propitious unto her, has wrought.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:21
verses.text: Wherefore this silence is called the Son of the right hand, which is, "Chusi, the son of Gemini".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:22
verses.text: "O Lord my God, in Thee have I hoped: save me from all them that persecute me, and deliver me".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:23
verses.text: As one to whom, already perfected, all the war and enmity of vice being overcome, there remaineth no enemy but the envious devil, he says, "Save me from all them that persecute me, and deliver me : lest at any time he tear my soul as a lion".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:24
verses.text: The Apostle says, "Your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:25
verses.text: Therefore when the Psalmist said in the plural number, "Save me from all them that persecute me:" he afterwards introduced the singular, saying, "lest at any time he tear my soul as a lion".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:26
verses.text: For he does not say, lest at any time they tear: he knew what enemy and violent adversary of the perfect soul remained.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:27
verses.text: "Whilst there be none to redeem, nor to save:" that is, lest he tear me, whilst Thou redeemest not, nor savest.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:28
verses.text: For, if God redeem not, nor save, he tears.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:29
verses.text: And that it might be clear that the already perfect soul, which is to be on her guard against the most insidious snares of the devil only, says this, see what follows.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:30
verses.text: "O Lord my God, if I have done this".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:31
verses.text: What is it that he calls "this"? Since he does not mention the sin by name, are we to understand sin generally? If this sense displease us, we may take that to be meant which follows: as if we had asked, what is this that you say, "this"? He answers, "If there be iniquity in my hands".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:32
verses.text: Now then it is clear that it is said of all sin, "If I have repaid them that recompense me evil".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:33
verses.text: Which none can say with truth, but the perfect.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:34
verses.text: For so the Lord says, "Be ye perfect, as your Father which is in heaven; who maketh His sun to rise upon the good and the evil, and raineth on the just and the unjust".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:35
verses.text: He then who repayeth not them that recompense evil, is perfect.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:36
verses.text: When therefore the perfect soul prays "for the words of Chusi, the son of Jemini," that is, for the knowledge of that secret and silence, which the Lord, favourable to us and merciful, wrought for our salvation, so as to endure, and with all patience bear, the guiles of this betrayer: as if He should say to this perfect soul, explaining the design of this secret, For thee ungodly and a sinner, that thine iniquities might be washed away by My blood-shedding, in great silence and great patience I bore with My betrayer; wilt not thou imitate me, that thou too mayest not repay evil for evil? Considering then, and understanding what the Lord has done for him, and by His example going on to perfection, the Psalmist says, "If I have repaid them that recompense me evil:" that is, if I have not done what Thou hast taught me by Thy example: "may I therefore fall by mine enemies empty".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:37
verses.text: And he says well, not, If I have repaid them that do me evil; but, who "recompense".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:38
verses.text: For who so recompenseth, had received somewhat already.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:39
verses.text: Now it is an instance of greater patience, not even to repay him evil, who after receiving benefits returns evil for good, than if without receiving any previous benefit he had had a mind to injure.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:40
verses.text: If therefore he says, "I have repaid them that recompense me evil:" that is, If I have not imitated Thee in that silence, that is, in Thy patience, which Thou hast wrought for me, "may I fall by mine enemies empty".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:41
verses.text: For he is an empty boaster, who, being himself a man, desires to avenge himself on a man; and whilst he openly seeks to overcome a man, is secretly himself overcome by the devil, rendered empty by vain and proud joy, because he could not, as it were, be conquered.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:42
verses.text: The Psalmist knows then where a greater victory may be obtained, and where "the Father which seeth in secret will reward".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:43
verses.text: Lest then he repay them that recompense evil, he overcomes his anger rather than another man, being instructed too by those writings, wherein it is written, "Better is he that overcometh his anger, than he that taketh a city".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:44
verses.text: "If I have repaid them that recompense me evil, may I therefore fall by my enemies empty".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:45
verses.text: He seems to swear by way of execration, which is the heaviest kind of oath, as when one says, If I have done so and so, may I suffer so and so.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:46
verses.text: But swearing in a swearer's mouth is one thing, in a prophet's meaning another.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:47
verses.text: For here he mentions what will really befall men who repay them that recompense evil; not what, as by an oath, he would imprecate on himself or any other.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:48
verses.text: "Let the enemy" therefore "persecute my soul and take it".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:49
verses.text: By again naming the enemy in the singular number, he more and more clearly points out him whom he spoke of above as a lion.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:50
verses.text: For he persecutes the soul, and if he has deceived it, will take it.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:51
verses.text: For the limit of men's rage is the destruction of the body; but the soul, after this visible death, they cannot keep in their power: whereas whatever souls the devil shall have taken by his persecutions, he will keep.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:52
verses.text: "And let him tread my life upon the earth:" that is, by treading let him make my life earth, that is to say, his food.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:53
verses.text: For he is not only called a lion, but a serpent too, to whom it was said, "Earth shalt thou eat".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:54
verses.text: And to the sinner was it said, "Earth thou art, and into earth shalt thou go".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:55
verses.text: "And let him bring down my glory to the dust".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:56
verses.text: This is that dust which "the wind casteth forth from the face of the earth," to wit, vain and silly boasting of the proud, puffed up, not of solid weight, as a cloud of dust carried away by the wind.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:57
verses.text: Justly then has he here spoken of the glory, which he would not have brought down to dust.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:58
verses.text: For he would have it solidly established in conscience before God, where there is no boasting.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:59
verses.text: "He that glorieth," saith the Apostle, "let him glory in the Lord".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:60
verses.text: This solidity is brought down to the dust if one through pride despising the secrecy of conscience, where God only proves a man, desires to glory before men.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:61
verses.text: Hence comes what the Psalmist elsewhere says, "God shall bruise the bones of them that please men".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:62
verses.text: Now he that has well learnt or experienced the steps in overcoming vices, knows that this vice of empty glory is either alone, or more than all, to be shunned by the perfect.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:63
verses.text: For that by which the soul first fell, she overcomes the last.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:64
verses.text: "For the beginning of all sin is pride:" and again, "The beginning of man's pride is to depart from God".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:65
verses.text: "Arise, O Lord, in Thine anger".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:66
verses.text: Why yet does he, who we say is perfect, incite God to anger? Must we not see, whether he rather be not perfect, who, when he was being stoned, said, "O Lord, lay not this sin to their charge"? Or does the Psalmist pray thus not against men, but against the devil and his angels, whose possession sinners and the ungodly are? He then does not pray against him in wrath, but in mercy, whosoever prays that that possession may be taken from him by that Lord "who justifieth the ungodly".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:67
verses.text: For when the ungodly is justified, from ungodly he is made just, and from being the possession of the devil he passes into the temple of God.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:68
verses.text: And since it is a punishment that a possession, in which one longs to have rule, should be taken away from him: this punishment, that he should cease to possess those whom he now possesses, the Psalmist calls the anger of God against the devil.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:69
verses.text: "Arise, O Lord; in Thine anger".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:70
verses.text: "Arise" (he has used it as "appear"), in words, that is, human and obscure; as though God sleeps, when He is unrecognised and hidden in His secret workings.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:71
verses.text: "Be exalted in the borders of mine enemies".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:72
verses.text: He means by borders the possession itself, in which he wishes that God should be exalted, that is, be honoured and glorified, rather than the devil, while the ungodly are justified and praise God.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:73
verses.text: "And arise, O Lord my God, in the commandment that Thou hast given:" that is, since Thou hast enjoined humility, appear in humility; and first fulfil what Thou hast enjoined; that men by Thy example overcoming pride may not be possessed of the devil, who against Thy commandments advised to pride, saying, "Eat, and your eyes shall be opened, and ye shall be as gods".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:74
verses.text: "And the congregation of the people shall surround Thee".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:75
verses.text: This may be understood two ways.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:76
verses.text: For the congregation of the people can be taken, either of them that believe, or of them that persecute, both of which took place in the same humiliation of our Lord: in contempt of which the multitude of them that persecute surrounded Him; concerning which it is said, "Why have the heathen raged, and the people meditated vain things?"  But of them that believe through His humiliation the multitude so surrounded Him, that it could be said with the greatest truth, "blindness in part is happened unto Israel, that the fulness of the Gentiles might come in:" and again, "Ask of me, and I will give Thee the Gentiles for Thine inheritance, and the boundaries of the earth for Thy possession".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:77
verses.text: "And for their sakes return Thou on high:" that is, for the sake of this congregation return Thou on high: which He is understood to have done by His resurrection and ascension into heaven.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:78
verses.text: For being thus glorified He gave the Holy Ghost, which before His exaltation could not be given, as it is written in the Gospel, "for the Holy Ghost was not yet given, because that Jesus was not yet glorified".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:79
verses.text: Having then returned on high for the sake of the congregation of the people, He sent the Holy Ghost: by whom the preachers of the Gospel being filled, filled the whole world with Churches.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:80
verses.text: It can be taken also in this sense: "Arise, O Lord, in Thine anger, and be exalted in the borders of mine enemies:" that is, arise in Thine anger, and let not mine enemies understand Thee; so that to "be exalted," should be this, become high, that Thou mayest not be understood; which has reference to the silence spoken of above.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:81
verses.text: For it is of this exaltation thus said in another Psalm, "And He ascended upon Cherubim, and flew:" and, "He made darkness His secret place".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:82
verses.text: In which exaltation, or concealment, when for their sins' desert they shall not understand Thee, who shall crucify Thee, "the congregation" of believers "shall surround Thee".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:83
verses.text: For in His very humiliation He was exalted, that is, was not understood.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:84
verses.text: So that, "And arise, O Lord my God, in the commandment that Thou hast given:" may have reference to this, that is, when Thou showest Thyself, be high or deep that mine enemies may not understand Thee.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:85
verses.text: Now sinners are the enemies of the just man, and the ungodly of the godly man.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:86
verses.text: "And the congregation of the people shall surround Thee:" that is, by this very circumstance, that those who crucify Thee understand Thee not, the Gentiles shall believe on Thee, and so "shall the congregation of the people surround Thee".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:87
verses.text: But what follows, if this be the true meaning, has in it more pain, that it begins already to be perceived, than joy that it is understood.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:88
verses.text: For it follows, "and for their sakes return Thou on high," that is, and for the sake of this congregation of the human race, wherewith the Churches are crowded, return Thou on high, that is, again cease to be understood.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:89
verses.text: What then is, "and for their sakes," but that this congregation too will offend Thee, so that Thou mayest most truly foretell and say, "Thinkest Thou when the Son of man shall come, He will find faith on the earth?" Again, of the false prophets, who are understood to be heretics, He says, "Because of their iniquity the love of many shall wax cold".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:90
verses.text: Since then even in the Churches, that is, in that congregation of peoples and nations, where the Christian name has most widely spread, there shall be so great abundance of sinners, which is already, in great measure, perceived; is not that famine of the word here predicted, which has been threatened by another prophet also? Is it not too for this congregation's sake, who, by their sins, are estranging from themselves that light of truth, that God returns on high, that is, so that faith, pure and cleansed from the corruption of all perverse opinions, is held and received, either not at all, or by the very few of whom it was said, "Blessed is he that shall endure to the end, the same shall be saved"?  Not without cause then is it said, "and for the sake of this" congregation "return Thou on high:" that is, again withdraw into the depth of Thy secrecy, even for the sake of this congregation of the peoples, that hath Thy name, and doeth not Thy deeds.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:91
verses.text: But whether the former exposition of this place, or this last be the more suitable, without prejudice to any one better, or equal, or as good, it follows very consistently, "the Lord judgeth the people".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:92
verses.text: For whether He returned on high, when, after the resurrection, He ascended into heaven, well does it follow, "The Lord judgeth the people:" for that He will come from thence to judge the quick and the dead.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:93
verses.text: Or whether He return on high, when the understanding of the truth leaves sinful Christians, for that of His coming it has been said, "Thinkest thou the Son of Man on His coming will find faith on the earth?" "The Lord" then "judgeth the people".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:94
verses.text: What Lord, but Jesus Christ? "For the Father judgeth no man, but hath committed all judgment unto the Son".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:95
verses.text: Wherefore this soul which prayeth perfectly, see how she fears not the day of judgment, and with a truly secure longing says in her prayer, "Thy kingdo m come: judge me," she says, "O Lord, according to my righteousness".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:96
verses.text: In the former Psalm a weak one was entreating, imploring rather the mercy of God, than mentioning any desert of his own: since the Son of God came "to call sinners to repentance".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:97
verses.text: Therefore he had there said, "Save me, O Lord, for Thy mercy's sake;" that is, not for my desert's sake.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:98
verses.text: But now, since being called he hath held and kept the commandments which he received, he is bold to say, "Judge me, O Lord, according to my righteousness, and according to my harmlessness, that is upon me".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:99
verses.text: This is true harmlessness, which harms not even an enemy.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:100
verses.text: Accordingly, well does he require to be judged according to his harmlessness, who could say with truth, "If I have repaid them that recompense me evil".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:101
verses.text: As for what he added, "that is upon me," it can refer not only to harmlessness, but can be understood also with reference to righteousness; that the sense should be this, Judge me, O Lord, according to my righteousness, and according to my harmlessness, which righteousness and harmlessness is upon me.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:102
verses.text: By which addition he shows that this very thing, that the soul is righteous and harmless, she has not by herself, but by God who giveth brightness and light.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:103
verses.text: For of this he says in another Psalm, "Thou, O Lord, wilt light my candle".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:104
verses.text: And of John it is said, that "he was not the light, but bore witness of the light".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:105
verses.text: "He was a burning and shining candle".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:106
verses.text: That light then, whence souls, as candles, are kindled, shines forth not with borrowed, but with original, brightness, which light is truth itself.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:107
verses.text: It is then so said, "According to my righteousness, and according to my harmlessness, that is upon me," as if a burning and shining candle should say, Judge me according to the flame which is upon me, that is, not that wherewith I am myself, but that whereby I shine enkindled of thee.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:108
verses.text: "But let the wickedness of sinners be consummated".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:109
verses.text: He says, "be consummated," be completed, according to that in the Apocalypse, "Let the righteous become more righteous, and let the filthy be filthy still".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:110
verses.text: For the wickedness of those men appears consummate, who crucified the Son of God; but greater is theirs who will not live uprightly, and hate the precepts of truth, for whom the Son of God was crucified.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:111
verses.text: "Let the wickedness of sinners," then he says, "be consummated," that is, arrive at the height of wickedness, that just judgment may be able to come at once.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:112
verses.text: But since it is not only said, "Let the filthy be filthy still;" but it is said also, "Let the righteous become more righteous;" he joins on the words, "And Thou shalt direct the righteous, O God, who searcheth the hearts and reins".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:113
verses.text: How then can the righteous be directed but in secret? when even by means of those things which, in the commencement of the Christian ages, when as yet the saints were oppressed by the persecution of the men of this world, appeared marvellous to men, now that the Christian name has begun to be in such high dignity, hypocrisy, that is pretence, has increased; of those, I mean, who by the Christian profession had rather please men than God.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:114
verses.text: How then is the righteous man directed in so great confusion of pretence, save whilst God searcheth the hearts and reins; seeing all men's thoughts, which are meant by the word heart; and their delights, which are understood by the word reins? For the delight in things temporal and earthly is rightly ascribed to the reins; for that it is both the lower part of man, and that region where the pleasure of carnal generation dwells, through which man's nature is transferred into this life of care, and deceiving joy, by the succession of the race.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:115
verses.text: God then, searching our heart, and perceiving that it is there where our treasure is, that is, in heaven; searching also the reins, and perceiving that we do not assent to flesh and blood, but delight ourselves in the Lord, directs the righteous man in his inward conscience before Him, where no man seeth, but He alone who perceiveth what each man thinketh, and what delighteth each.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:116
verses.text: For delight is the end of care; because to this end does each man strive by care and thought, that he may attain to his delight.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:117
verses.text: He therefore seeth our cares, who searcheth the heart.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:118
verses.text: He seeth too the ends of cares, that is delights, who narrowly searcheth the reins; that when He shall find that our cares incline neither to the lust of the flesh, nor to the lust of the eyes, nor to the pride of life, all which pass away as a shadow, but that they are raised upward to the joys of things eternal, which are spoilt by no change, He may direct the righteous, even He, the God who searcheth the hearts and reins.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:119
verses.text: For our works, which we do in deeds and words, may be known unto men; but with what mind they are done, and to what end we would attain by means of them, He alone knoweth, the God who searcheth the hearts and reins.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:120
verses.text: "My righteous help is from the Lord, who maketh whole the upright in heart".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:121
verses.text: The offices of medicine are twofold, on the curing infirmity, the other the preserving health.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:122
verses.text: According to the first it was said in the preceding Psalm, "Have mercy on me, O Lord, for I am weak;" according to the second it is said in this Psalm, "If there be iniquity in my hands, if I have repaid them that recompense me evil, may I therefore fall by my enemies empty".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:123
verses.text: For there the weak prays that he may be delivered, here one already whole that he may not change for the worse.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:124
verses.text: According to the one it is there said, "Make me whole for Thy mercy's sake;" according to this other it is here said, "Judge me, O Lord, according to my righteousness".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:125
verses.text: For there he asks for a remedy to escape from disease; but here for protection from falling into disease.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:126
verses.text: According to the former it is said, "Make me whole, O Lord, according to Thy mercy:" according to the latter it is said, "My righteous help is from the Lord, who maketh whole the upright in heart".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:127
verses.text: Both the one and the other maketh men whole; but the former removes them from sickness into health, the latter preserves them in this health.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:128
verses.text: Therefore there the help is merciful, because the sinner hath no desert, who as yet longeth to be justified, "believing on Him who justifieth the ungodly;" but here the help is righteous, because it is given to one already righteous.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:129
verses.text: Let the sinner then who said, "I am weak," say in the first place, "Make me whole, O Lord, for Thy mercy's sake;" and here let the righteous man, who said, "If I have repaid them that recompense me evil," say, "My righteous help is from the Lord, who maketh whole the upright in heart".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:130
verses.text: For if he sets forth the medicine, by which we may be healed when weak, how much more that by which we may be kept in health.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:131
verses.text: For if "while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us, how much more being now justified shall we be kept whole from wrath through Him".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:132
verses.text: "My righteous help is from the Lord, who maketh whole the upright in heart".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:133
verses.text: God, who searcheth the hearts and reins, directeth the righteous; but with righteous help maketh He whole the upright in heart.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:134
verses.text: He doth not as He searcheth the hearts and reins, so make whole the upright in heart and reins; for the thoughts are both bad in a depraved heart, and good in an upright heart; but delights which are not good belong to the reins, for they are more low and earthly; but those that are good not to the reins, but to the heart itself.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:135
verses.text: Wherefore men cannot be so called upright in reins, as they are called upright in heart, since where the thought is, there at once the delight is too; which cannot be, unless when things divine and eternal are thought of.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:136
verses.text: "Thou hast given," he says, "joy in my heart," when he had said, "The light of Thy countenance has been stamped on us, O Lord".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:137
verses.text: For although the phantoms of things temporal, which the mind falsely pictures to itself, when tossed by vain and mortal hope, to vain imagination oftentimes bring a delirious and maddened joy; yet this delight must be attributed not to the heart, but to the reins; for all these imaginations have been drawn from lower, that is, earthly and carnal things.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:138
verses.text: Hence it comes, that God, who searcheth the hearts and reins, and perceiveth in the heart upright thoughts, in the reins no delights, affordeth righteous help to the upright in hea rt, where heavenly delights are coupled with clean thoughts.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:139
verses.text: And therefore when in another Psalm he had said, "Moreover even to-night my reins have chided me;" he went on to say as touching help, "I foresaw the Lord alway in my sight, for He is on my right hand, that I should not be moved".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:140
verses.text: Where he shows that he suffered suggestions only from the reins, not delights as well; for he had suffered these, then he would of course be moved.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:141
verses.text: But he said, "The Lord is on my right hand, that I should not be moved;" and then he adds, "Wherefore was my heart delighted;" that the reins should have been able to chide, not delight him.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:142
verses.text: The delight accordingly was produced not in the reins, but there, where against the chiding of the reins God was foreseen to be on the right hand, that is, in the heart.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:143
verses.text: "God the righteous judge, strong (in endurance) and long-suffering".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:144
verses.text: What God is judge, but the Lord, who judgeth the people? He is righteous; who "shall render to every man according to his works".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:145
verses.text: He is strong (in endurance); who, being most powerful, for our salvation bore even with ungodly persecutors.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 7:146
