verses.text: He is taught to love the better, by the bitterness of the worse; lest going a traveller to his country, he choose the inn instead of his own home.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:69
verses.text: But why this? Because He "scourgeth every son whom He receiveth".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:70
verses.text: Why this? Because to men sinning was it said, "In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:71
verses.text: Therefore because all these chastisements, in which all our bed is turned in our infirmity, man ought to acknowledge that he suffers for sin; let him turn himself, and say what follows: "I said, Lord, be merciful unto me; heal my soul, for I have sinned against Thee".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:72
verses.text: O Lord, by tribulations do Thou exercise me; to be scourged Thou judgest every son whom Thou wilt receive, who sparedst not even the Only-Begotten.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:73
verses.text: He indeed without sin was scourged; but I say, "I have sinned against Thee".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:74
verses.text: "Mine enemies speak evil of Me, When He shall die, then shall His Name perish".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:75
verses.text: Of this we have already spoken, and from this began.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:76
verses.text: "And entered in to see".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:77
verses.text: What Christ suffered, that suffereth also the Church; what the Head suffered, that suffer also the Members.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:78
verses.text: "For the disciple is not above his Master, nor the servant above his Lord".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:79
verses.text: If to Christ's Members thou belongest, come within, cling to the Head.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:80
verses.text: Endure the tares if thou art wheat, endure the chaff if thou art grain Endure the bad fish within the net if thou art a good fish.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:81
verses.text: Wherefore before the time of winnowing dost thou fly away? Wherefore before the time of harvest, dost thou root up the corn also with thyself? Wherefore before thou art come to the shore, hast thou broken the nets? "They go abroad, and tell it".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:82
verses.text: "All mine enemies whisper against Me unto the same thing".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:83
verses.text: Against Me all unto the same thing.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:84
verses.text: How much better with me unto the same thing, than against me "unto the same thing".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:85
verses.text: What is, "Against me unto the same thing"? With one counsel, with one conspiring.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:86
verses.text: Christ then speaketh unto thee, Ye consent against Me, consent ye to Me: why against Me? wherefore not with Me? That same thing if ye had always had, ye had not divided you into schisms.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:87
verses.text: For, saith the Apostle, "I beseech you, brethren, that ye all speak the same thing, and that there be no division among you".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:88
verses.text: "All mine enemies whisper against Me unto the same thing:" against Me do they "devise evil to Me".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:89
verses.text: To themselves rather, for "they have gathered iniquity to themselves;" but therefore to Me, because by their intention they are to be weighed: for not because to do nothing was in their power, to do nothing was in their will.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:90
verses.text: For the devil lusted to extinguish Christ, and Judas would slay Christ; yet Christ slain and rising again, we are made alive, but to the devil and to Judas is rendered the reward of their evil will, not of our salvation.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:91
verses.text: The intention wherewith they spake, not what they spake, did He consider, who related that they spake evil of Him, "Against Me they devised evil to Me".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:92
verses.text: And what evil to Christ, to the Martyrs what evil? All hath God turned to good.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:93
verses.text: "An ungodly word do they set forth against Me".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:94
verses.text: What sort of ungodly word? Listen to the Head Itself.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:95
verses.text: "Come, let us kill Him, and the inheritance shall be ours".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:96
verses.text: Fools! How shall the inheritance be yours? Because ye killed Him? Lo! ye even killed Him; yet shall not the inheritance be yours.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:97
verses.text: "Shall not He that sleepeth add this also, that He rise again"? When ye exulted that ye had slain Him, He slept; for He saith in another Psalm, "I slept".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:98
verses.text: They raged and would slay Me; "I slept".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:99
verses.text: If I had not willed, I had not even slept.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:100
verses.text: "I slept," because "I have power to lay down My life, and I have power to take it again".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:101
verses.text: "I laid Me down and slept, and rose up again".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:102
verses.text: Rage then the Jews; be "the earth given into the hands of the wicked," be the flesh left to the hands of persecutors, let them on wood suspend it, with nails transfix it, with a spear pierce it.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:103
verses.text: "Shall He that sleepeth, not add this, that He rise up again?" Wherefore slept He? Because "Adam is the figure of Him that was to come".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:104
verses.text: And Adam slept, when out of his side was made Eve Adam in the figure of Christ, Eve in the figure of the Church; whence she was called "the mother of all living".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:105
verses.text: When was Eve created? While Adam slept.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:106
verses.text: When out of Christ's side flowed the Sacraments of the Church? While He slept upon the Cross.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:107
verses.text: "The man of My peace, in whom I trusted, which did eat of My bread, hath enlarged his heel against Me" : hath raised up his foot against Me: would trample upon Me.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:108
verses.text: Who is this man of His peace? Judas.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:109
verses.text: And in him did Christ trust, that He said, "in whom I trusted"? Did He not know him from the beginning? Did He not before he was born know that he would be? Had He not said to all His disciples, "I have chosen you twelve, and one of you is a devil"? How then trusted He in him, but that He is in His Members, and that because many faithful trusted in Judas, the Lord transferred this to Himself?"The man of My peace, in whom I trusted, which did eat of My bread".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:110
verses.text: How showed He him in His Passion? By the words of His prophecy: by the sop He marked Him out, that it might appear said of him, "Which did eat of My bread".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:111
verses.text: Again, when he came to betray Him, He granted him a kiss, that it might appear said of him, "The man of My peace".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:112
verses.text: "But Thou, O Lord, be merciful unto Me".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:113
verses.text: This is the person of a servant, this is the person of the needy and poor: for, "Blessed is he that understandeth upon the needy and poor One".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:114
verses.text: See, as it was spoken, "Be merciful unto Me, and raise Me up, and I will requite them," so is it done.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:115
verses.text: For the Jews slew Christ, lest they should lose their place Christ slain, they lost their place.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:116
verses.text: Rooted out of the kingdom were they, dispersed were they.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:117
verses.text: He, raised up, requited them tribulation, He requited them unto admonition, not yet unto condemnation.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:118
verses.text: For the city wherein the people raged, as a ramping and a roaring lion, crying out, "Crucify Him, Crucify Him," the Jews rooted out therefrom, hath now Christians, by not one Jew is inhabited There is planted the Church of Christ, whence were rooted out the thorns of the synagogue.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:119
verses.text: For truly this fire blazed "as the fire of thorns".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:120
verses.text: But the Lord was as a green tree.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:121
verses.text: This said Himself, when certain women mourned Christ as dying.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:122
verses.text: "For if they do these things in a green tree, what shall be done in a dry?" When can a green tree be consumed by the fire of thorns? For they blazed as fire among thorns.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:123
verses.text: Fire consumeth thorns, but whatsoever green tree it is applied to, is not easily kindled.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:124
verses.text: Yet lest ye think that God the Father of Christ could raise up Christ, that is, the Flesh of His Son, and that Christ Himself, though He be the Word equal with the Father, could not raise up His own Flesh; hear out of the Gospel, "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:125
verses.text: "But," said the Evangelist (lest even after this we should doubt), "He spake of the temple of His Body.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:126
verses.text: Raise Me up, and I will requite them".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:127
verses.text: "By this I know that Thou favourest Me, that Mine enemies shall not triumph over Me" (ver.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:128
verses.text: ) Because the Jews did triumph, when they saw Christ crucified; they thought that they had fulfilled their will to do Him hurt: the fruits of their cruelty they saw in effect, Christ hanging on the Cross: they shook their heads, saying, "If Thou be the Son of God, come down from the Cross".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:129
verses.text: He came not down, who could; His Potency He showed not, but patience taught.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:130
verses.text: For if, on their saying these things, He had come down from the Cross, He would have seemed as it were to yield to them insulting, and not being able to endure reproach, would have been believed conquered: more firm remained He upon the Cross, than they insulting; fixed was He, they wavering.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:131
verses.text: For therefore shook they their heads, because to the true Head they adhered not.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:132
verses.text: He taught us plainly patience.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:133
verses.text: For mightier is that which He did, who would not do what the Jews challenged.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:134
verses.text: For much mightier is it to rise from the sepulchre, than to come down from the Cross.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:135
verses.text: "That Mine enemies shall not triumph over Me".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:136
verses.text: They triumphed then at that time.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:137
verses.text: Christ rose again, Christ was glorified.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:138
verses.text: Now see they in His Name the human race converted: now let them insult, now shake the head: rather now let them fix the head, or if they shake the head, in wonder and admiration let them shake.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:139
verses.text: "But as for Me, Thou upholdest Me, because of Mine innocence".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:140
verses.text: Truly innocence; integrity without sin, requiting without debt, scourging without desert.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:141
verses.text: "Thou upholdest Me because of Mine innocence, and hast made Me strong in Thy sight for ever".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:142
verses.text: Thou hast made Me strong for ever, Thou madest Me weak for a time: Thou hast made Me strong in Thy sight, Thou madest Me weak in sight of men.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:143
verses.text: What then? Praise to Him, glory to Him.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:144
verses.text: "Blessed be the Lord God of Israel".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:145
verses.text: For He is the God of Israel, our God, the God of Jacob, the God of the younger son, the God of the younger people.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:146
verses.text: Let none say, Of the Jews said He this, I am not Israel; rather the Jews are not Israel.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:147
verses.text: For the elder son, he is the elder people reprobated; the younger, the people beloved.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:148
verses.text: "The elder shall serve the younger:" now is it fulfilled: now, brethren, the Jews serve us, they are as our satchellers, we studying, they carry our books.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:149
verses.text: Hear wherein the Jews serve us, and not without reason.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:150
verses.text: With them are the Law and the Prophets, in which Law, and in which Prophets, Christ is preached.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:151
verses.text: When we have to do with Pagans, and show this coming to pass in the Church of Christ, which before was predicted of the Name of Christ, of the Head and Body of Christ, lest they think that we have forged these predictions, and from things which have happened, as though they were future, had made them up, we bring forth the books of the Jews.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:152
verses.text: The Jews forsooth are our enemies, from an enemy's books convince we the adversaryIf any enemy clamour and say, "Ye for yourselves have forged prophecies;" be the books of the Jews brought forth, because the elder shall serve the younger.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 41:153
verses.text: Therein let them read those predictions, which now we see fulfilled; and let us all say, "Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, from everlasting to everlasting, and all the people shall say, So be it, So be it".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:1
verses.text: Psalm XLII.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:2
verses.text: We have undertaken the exposition of a P salm corresponding to your own "longings," on which we propose to speak to you.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:3
verses.text: For the Psalm itself begins with a certain pious "longing;" and he who sings so, says, "Like as the hart desireth the water-brooks, so longeth my soul after Thee, O God".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:4
verses.text: Who is it then that saith this? It is ourselves, if we be but willing! And why ask, who it is other than thyself, when it is in thy power to be the thing which thou art asking about? It is not however one individual, but it is "One Body;" but "Christ's Body is the Church".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:5
verses.text: Such "longing" indeed is not found in all who enter the Church: let all however who have "tasted" the sweetness "of the Lord," and who own in Christ that for which they have a relish, think that they are not the only ones; but that there are such seeds scattered throughout "the field" of the Lord, this whole earth: and that there is a certain Christian unity, whose voice thus speaks, "Like as the hart desireth the water-brooks, so longeth my soul after Thee, O God".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:6
verses.text: And indeed it is not ill understood as the cry of those, who being as yet  Catechumens, are hastening to the grace of the holy Font.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:7
verses.text: On which account too this Psalm is ordinarily chanted on those occasions, that they may long for the Fountain of remission of sins, even "as the hart for the water-brooks".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:8
verses.text: Let this be allowed; and this meaning retain its place in the Church; a place both truthful and sanctioned by usage Nevertheless, it appears to me, my brethren, that such "a longing" is not fully satisfied even in the faithful in Baptism: but that haply, if they know where they are sojourning, and whither they have to remove from hence, their "longing" is kindled in even greater intensity.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:9
verses.text: The title then of it is, "On the end: a Psalm for understanding for the sons of Korah".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:10
verses.text: We have met with the sons of Korah in other titles of Psalms: and remember to have discussed and stated already the meaning of this name.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:11
verses.text: Yet we must even now take notice of this title in such a way, that what we have said already should be no prejudice against our saying it again: for all were not present in every place where we said it.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:12
verses.text: Now Korah may have been, as indeed he was, a certain definite person; and have had sons, who might be called "the sons of Korah;" let us however search for the secret of which this is the sacrament, that this name may bring to light the mystery with which it is pregnant.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:13
verses.text: For there is some great mystery in the matter that the name "sons of Korah" is given to Christians.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:14
verses.text: Why "sons of Korah"? They are "sons of the bridegroom, sons of Christ".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:15
verses.text: Why then does "Korah" stand for Christ? Because "Korah" is equivalent to "Calvaria".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:16
verses.text: Therefore, the "sons of the bridegroom," the sons of His Passion, the sons redeemed by His Blood, the sons of His Cross, who bear on their forehead that whic h His enemies  erected on Calvary, are called "the sons of Korah;" to them is this Psalm su ng as a Psalm for "understanding".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:17
verses.text: Let then our understanding be roused: and if the Psalm be sung to us, let us follow it with our "understanding".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:18
verses.text: Run to the brooks; long after the water-brooks.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:19
verses.text: "With God is the fountain of Life;" a "fountain" that shall never be dried up: in His "Light" is a Light that shall never be darkened.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:20
verses.text: Long thou for this light: for a certain fountain, a certain light, such as thy bodily eyes know not; a light to see which the inward eye must be prepared; a fountain, to drink of which the inward thirst is to be kindled.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:21
verses.text: Run to the fountain; long for the fountain; but do it not anyhow, be not satisfied with running like any ordinary animal; run thou "like the hart".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:22
verses.text: What is meant by "like the hart"? Let there be no sloth in thy running; run with all thy might: long for the fountain with all thy might.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:23
verses.text: For we find in "the hart" an emblem of swiftness.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:24
verses.text: But perhaps Scripture meant us to consider in the stag not this point only, but another also.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:25
verses.text: Hear what else there is in the hart.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:26
verses.text: It destroys serpents, and after the killing of serpents, it is inflamed with thirst yet more violent; having destroyed serpents, it runs to "the water-brooks," with thirst more keen than before.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:27
verses.text: The serpents are thy vices, destroy the serpents of iniquity; then wilt thou long yet more for "the Fountain of Truth".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:28
verses.text: Perhaps avarice whispers in thine ear some dark counsel, hisses against the word of God, hisses against the commandment of God.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:29
verses.text: And since it is said to thee, "Disregard this or that thing," if thou prefer working iniquity to despising some temporal good, thou choosest to be bitten by a serpent, rather than destroy it.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:30
verses.text: Whilst, therefore, thou art yet indulgent to thy vice, thy covetousness or thy appetite, when am I to find in thee "a longing" such as this, that might make thee run to the water-brooks?.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:31
verses.text: There is another point to be observed in the hart.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:32
verses.text: It is reported of stagsthat when they either wander in the herds, or when they are swimming to reach some other parts of the earth, that they support the burdens of their heads on each other, in such a manner as that one takes the lead, and others follow, resting their heads upon him, as again others who follow do upon them, and others in succession to the very end of the herd; but the one who took the lead in bearing the burden of their heads, when tired, returns to the rear, and rests himself after his fatigue by supporting his head just as did the others; by thus supporting what is burdensome, each in turn, they both accomplish their journey, and do not abandon each other.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:33
verses.text: Are they not a kind of "harts" that the Apostle addresses, saying, "Bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the Law of Christ"?.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:34
verses.text: "My soul is athirst for the living God".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:35
verses.text: What I am saying, that "as the hart panteth after the water-brooks, so longs my soul after Thee, O God," means this, "My soul is athirst for the living God".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:36
verses.text: For what is it athirst? "When shall I come and appear before God?" This it is for which I am athirst, to "come and to appear before Him".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:37
verses.text: I am athirst in my pilgrimage, in my running; I shall be filled on my arrival.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:38
verses.text: But "When shall I come?" And this, which is soon in the sight of God, is late to our "longing".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:39
verses.text: "When shall I come and appear before God?" This too proceeds from that "longing," of which in another place comes that cry, "One thing have I desired of the Lord; that will I seek after; that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:40
verses.text: Wherefore so? "That I may behold" (he saith) "the beauty of the Lord".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:41
verses.text: "When shall I come and appear before the Lord?".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:42
verses.text: "My tears have been my meat day and night, while they daily say unto me, Where is thy God?".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:43
verses.text: My tears (he saith) have been not bitterness, but "my bread".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:44
verses.text: Those very tears were sweet unto me: being athirst for that fountain, inasmuch as I was not as yet able to drink of it, I have eagerly made my tears my meat.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:45
verses.text: For he said not, "My tears became my drink," lest he should seem to have longed for them, as for "the water-brooks:" but, still retaining that thirst wherewith I burn, and by which I am hurried away towards the water-brooks, "My tears became my meat," whilst I am not yet there And assuredly he does but the more thirst for the water-brooks from making his tears his meat.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:46
verses.text: "And they daily say unto me, Where is thy God?" For if a Pagan should say this to me, I cannot retort it upon him, saying, "Where is thine?" inasmuch as he points with his finger to some stone, and says, "Lo, there is my God!" When I have laughed at the stone, and he who pointed to it has been put to the blush, he raises his eyes from the stone, looks up to heaven, and perhaps says, pointing his finger to the Sun, "Behold there my God! Where, I pray, is your God?" He has found something to point out to the eyes of the flesh; whereas I, on my part, not that I have not a God to show to him, cannot show him what he has no eyes to see.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:47
verses.text: For he indeed could point out to my bodily eyes his God, the Sun; but what eyes hath he to which I might point out the Creator of the Sun?.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:48
verses.text: "I thought on these things, and poured out my soul above myself".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:49
verses.text: When would my soul attain to that object of its search, which is "above my soul," if my soul were not to "pour itself out above itself"? For were it to rest in itself, it would not see anything else beyond itself; and in seeing itself, would not, for all that, see God.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:50
verses.text: Let then my insulting enemies now say, "Where is thy God?" aye, let them say it! I, so long as I do not "see," so long as my happiness is postponed, make my tears my "bread day and night".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:51
verses.text: Let them still say, "Where is thy God?" I seek my God in every corporeal nature, terrestrial or celestial, and find Him not: I seek His Substance in my own soul, and I find it not, yet still I have thought on these things, and wishing to "see the invisible things of my God, being understood by the things made," I have poured forth my soul above myself, and there remains no longer any being for me to attain to, save my God.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:52
verses.text: For it is "there" is the "house of my God".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:53
verses.text: His dwelling-place is above my soul; from thence He beholds me; from thence He created me; from thence He directs me and provides for me; from thence he appeals to me, and calls me, and directs me; leads me in the way, and to the end of my way.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:54
verses.text: For when I was "pouring out my soul above myself," in order to reach my God, why did I do so? "For I will go into the place of Thy Tabernacle".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:55
verses.text: For I should be in error were I to seek for my God without "the place of His tabernacle".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:56
verses.text: "For I will go into the place of Thy wonderful tabernacle, even unto the house of God".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:57
verses.text: "I will go," he says, "into the place of the wonderful tabernacle, even unto the house of God!" For there are already many things that I admire in "the tabernacle".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:58
verses.text: See how great wonders I admire in the tabernacle! For God's tabernacle on earth is the faithful; I admire in them the obedience of even their bodily members: that in them "Sin does not reign so that they should obey its lusts; neither do they yield their members instruments of unrighteousness unto sin; but unto the living God in good works".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:59
verses.text: I admire the sight of the bodily members warring in the service of the soul that serves God.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:60
verses.text: And wonderful though the tabernacle be, yet when I come to "the house of God," I am even struck dumb with astonishment.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:61
verses.text: Of that "house" he speaks in another Psalm, after he had put a certain abstruse and difficult question to himself (viz.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:62
verses.text: , why is it that it generally goes well with the wicked on earth, and ill with the good?), saying, "I thought to know this; it is too painful for me, until I go into the sanctuary of God, and understand of the last things".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:63
verses.text: For it is there, in the sanctuary of God, in the house of God, is the fountain of "understanding".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:64
verses.text: There he "understood of the last things;" and solved the question concerning the prosperity of the unrighteous, and the sufferings of the righteous.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:65
verses.text: How does he solve it? Why, that the wicked, when reprieved here, are reserved for punishments without end; and the good when they suffer here, are being tried in order that they may in the end obtain the inheritance.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:66
verses.text: And it was in the sanctuary of God that he understood this, and "understood of the last things".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:67
verses.text: For he tells us of his progress, and of his guidance thither; as if we had been saying, "You are admiring the tabernacle here on earth; how came you to the sanctuary of the house of God?" he says, "In the voice of joy and praise; the sound of keeping holiday".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:68
verses.text: Here, when men keep festival simply for their own indulgence, it is their custom to place musical instruments, or to station a chorus of singers,  before their houses, or any kind of music that serves and allures to wantonness.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:69
verses.text: And when these are heard, what do we passers by say? "What is going on here?" And we are told in answer, that it is some festival.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:70
verses.text: "It is a birthday that is being celebrated" (say they), "there is a marriage here;" that those songs may not appear out of place, but the luxurious indulgence may be excused by the festive occasion.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:71
verses.text: In the "house of God" there is a never-ending festival: for there it is not an occasion celebrated once, and then to pass away The angelic choir makes an eternal "holiday:" the presence of God's face, joy that never fails.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:72
verses.text: This is a "holiday" of such a kind, as neither to be opened by any dawn, nor terminated by any evening.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:73
verses.text: From that everlasting perpetual festivity, a certain sweet and melodious strain strikes on the ears of the heart, provided only the world do not drown the sounds.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:74
verses.text: As he walks in this tabernacle, and contemplates God's wonderful works for the redemption of the faithful, the sound of that festivity charms his ears, and bears the "hart" away to "the water-brooks".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:75
verses.text: But seeing, brethren, so long as "we are at home in this body, we are absent from the Lord;" and "the corruptible body presseth down the soul, and the earthly tabernacle weigheth down the mind that museth on many things;" even though we have some way or other dispersed the clouds, by walking as "longing" leads us on, and for a brief while have come within reach of that sound, so that by an effort we may catch something from that "house of God," yet through the burden, so to speak, of our infirmity, we sink back to our usual level, and relapse to our ordinary state And just as there we found cause for rejoicing, so here there will not be wanting an occasion for sorrow.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:76
verses.text: For that hart that made "tears" its "bread day and night," borne along by "longing to the water-brooks" (that is, to the spiritual delights of God), "pouring forth his soul above himself," that he may attain to what is "above" his own soul, walking towards "the place of the wonderful tabernacle, even unto the house of God," and led on by the sweetness of that inward spiritual sound to feel contempt for all outward things, and be borne on to things spiritual, is but a mortal man still; is still groaning here, still bearing about the frailty of flesh, still in peril in the midst of the "offences" of this world.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:77
verses.text: He therefore glances back to himself, as if he were coming from that world; and says to himself, now placed in the midst of these sorrows, comparing these with the things, to see which he had entered in there, and after seeing which he had come forth from thence;  "Why art thou cast down, O my soul, and why dost thou disquiet me?".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:78
verses.text: Lo, we have just now been gladdened by certain inward delights: with the mind's eye we have been able to behold, though but with a momentary glance, something not susceptible of change: why dost thou still "disquiet me, why art thou" still "cast down"? For thou dost not doubt of thy God.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:79
verses.text: For now thou art not without somewhat to say to thyself, in answer to those who say, "Where is thy God?" I have now had the perception of something that is unchangeable; why dost thou disquiet me still?  "Hope in God".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:80
verses.text: Just as if his soul was silently replying to him, "Why do I disquiet thee, but because I am not yet there, where that delight is, to which I was, as it were, rapt for a moment? Am I already 'drinking' from this 'fountain' with nothing to fear?"Still "Hope in God," is his answer to the soul that disquiets him, and would fain account for her disquiet from the evils with which this world abounds.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:81
verses.text: In the mean while dwell in hope: for "hope that is seen is not hope; but if we hope for that we see not, then do we with patience wait for it".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:82
verses.text: "Hope in God".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:83
verses.text: Why "hope"? "For I will confess unto Him".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:84
verses.text: What wilt thou "confess"? "My God is the saving health of my countenance".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:85
verses.text: My "health" (my salvation) cannot be from myself; this it is that I will say, that I will "confess".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:86
verses.text: It is my God that is "the saving health of my countenance".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:87
verses.text: For to account for his fears, in the midst of those things, which he now knows, having come after a sort to the "understanding" of them, he has been looking behind him again in anxiety, lest the enemy be stealing upon him: he cannot yet say, "I am made whole every whit".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:88
verses.text: For having but "the first-fruits of the Spirit, we groan within ourselves; waiting for the adoption, to wit, the redemption of the body".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:89
verses.text: When that "health" (that salvation) is perfected in us, then shall we be living in the house of God for ever, and praising for ever Him to whom it was said, "Blessed are they that dwell in Thy house, they will be praising Thee world without end".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:90
verses.text: This is not so yet, because the salvation which is promised, is not as yet in being; but it is "in hope" that I confess unto God, and say, "My God is the saving health of my countenance".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:91
verses.text: For it is "in hope" that "we are saved; but hope that is seen, is not hope".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:92
verses.text: "My soul is disquieted on account of myself".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:93
verses.text: Is it disquieted on account of God? It is on my own account it is disquieted.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:94
verses.text: By the Unchangeable it was revived; it is by the changeable it is disquieted.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:95
verses.text: I know that the righteousness of God remaineth; whether my own will remain stedfast, I know not.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:96
verses.text: For I am alarmed by the Apostle's saying, "Let him that thinketh he standeth, take heed lest he fall".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:97
verses.text: Therefore since "there is no soundness in me for myself," there is no hope either for me of myself.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:98
verses.text: "My soul is disquieted on account of myself".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:99
verses.text: "Therefore I remember Thee, O Lord, from the land of Jordan, and from the little hill of Hermon".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:100
verses.text: From whence did I remember thee? From the "little hill," and from the "land of Jordan".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:101
verses.text: Perhaps from Baptism, where the remission of sins is given.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:102
verses.text: For no one runs to the remission of sins, except he who is dissatisfied with himself; no one runs to the remission of sins, but he who confesses himself a sinner; no one confesses himself a sinner, except by humbling himself before God.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:103
verses.text: Therefore it is from "the land of Jordan I have remembered thee, and from the hill;" observe, not "of the great hill," that thou mayest make of the "little hill" a great one: for "whoso exalteth himself shall be abased, and whoso humbleth himself shall be exalted".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:104
verses.text: If you would also ask the meanings of the names, Jordan means "their descent".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:105
verses.text: Descend then, that thou mayest be "lifted up:" be not lifted up, lest thou be cast down.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:106
verses.text: "And the little hill of Hermon".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:107
verses.text: Hermon means "anathematizing".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:108
verses.text: Anathematize thyself, by being displeased with thyself; for if thou art pleased with thyself, God will be displeased with thee.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:109
verses.text: Because then God gives us all good things, because He Himself is good, not because we are worthy of it; because He is merciful, not because we have in anything deserved it; it is from "the land of Jordan, and from Hermon," that I remember thee.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:110
verses.text: And because he so remembers with humility, he shall earn his exaltation to fruition, for he is not "exalted" in himself, who "glories in the Lord".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:111
verses.text: "Deep calleth unto deep with the voice of thy water-spouts".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:112
verses.text: I may perhaps finish the Psalm, aided as I am by your attention, whose fervour I perceive.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:113
verses.text: As for your fatigue in hearing, I am not greatly solicitous, since you see me also, who speak, toiling in the heat of these exertions Assuredly it is from your seeing me labouring, that you labour with me: for I am labouring not for myself, but for you.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:114
verses.text: "Deep calleth unto deep with the voice of thy water-spouts".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:115
verses.text: It was God whom he addressed, who "remembered him from the land of Jordan and Hermon".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:116
verses.text: It was in wonder and admiration he spake this: "Abyss calleth unto abyss with the voice of Thy water-spouts".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:117
verses.text: What abyss is this that calls, and to what other abyss? Justly, because the "understanding"  spoken of is an "abyss".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:118
verses.text: For an "abyss" is a depth that cannot be reached or comprehended; and it is principally applied to a great body of water.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:119
verses.text: For there is a "depth," a "profound," the bottom of which cannot be reached by sounding.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:120
verses.text: Furthermore, it is said in a certain passage, "Thy judgments are a mighty abyss," Scripture meaning to suggest that the judgments of God are incomprehensible.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:121
verses.text: What then is the "abyss" that calls, and to what other "abyss" does it call? If by "abyss" we understand a great depth, is not man's heart, do you not suppose, "an abyss"? For what is there more profound than that "abyss"? Men may speak, may be seen by the operations of their members, may be heard speaking in conversation: but whose thought is penetrated, whose heart seen into? What he is inwardly engaged on, what he is inwardly capable of, what he is inwardly doing or what purposing, what he is inwardly wishing to happen, or not to happen, who shall comprehend? I think an "abyss" may not unreasonably be understood of man, of whom it is said elsewhere, "Man shall come to a deep heart, and God shall be exalted".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:122
verses.text: If man then is an "abyss," in what way doth "abyss" call on "abyss"? Does man "call on" man as God is called upon? No, but "calls on" is equivalent to "calls to him".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:123
verses.text: For it was said of a certain person, he calls on death; that is, lives in such a way as to be inviting death; for there is no man at all who puts up a prayer, and calls expressly on death: but men by evil-living invite death.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:124
verses.text: "Deep calls on deep," then, is, "man calls to man".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:125
verses.text: Thus is it wisdom is learnt, and thus faith, when "man calls to man".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:126
verses.text: The holy preachers of God's word call on the "deep:" are they not themselves "a deep" also?.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:127
verses.text: "Deep calleth to deep with the voice of Thy water-spouts".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:128
verses.text: I, who tremble all over, when my soul was disquieted on account of myself, feared greatly on account of Thy "judgments".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:129
verses.text: Are those judgments slight ones? They are great ones, severe, hard to bear; but would they were all.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:130
verses.text: "Deep calls to deep with the voice of Thy water-spouts," in that Thou threatenest, Thou sayest, that there is another condemnation in store even after those sufferings.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:131
verses.text: "Deep calls on deep with the voice of Thy water-spouts".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:132
verses.text: "Whither then shall I go from Thy presence? And whither shall I flee from Thy Spirit?" seeing that deep calls to deep, and after those sufferings severer ones are to be dreaded.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:133
verses.text: "All Thy overhangings and Thy waves are come upon me".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:134
verses.text: The "waves" in what I already feel, the "overhangings" in that Thou denouncest.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:135
verses.text: All my sufferings are Thy waves; all Thy denouncements of judgments are Thy "overhangings".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:136
verses.text: In the "waves" that deep "calleth;" in the "overhangings" is the other "deep" which it "calls to".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:137
verses.text: In this that I suffer are all Thy waves; in the severer punishment that Thou threatenest, all Thy "overhangings" are come unto me.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:138
verses.text: For He who threatens does not let His judgments fall upon us, but keeps them suspended over us But inasmuch as Thou sittest at liberty, I have thus spoken unto my soul.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:139
verses.text: "Hope in God: for I will confess unto Him.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:140
verses.text: My God is the saving health of my countenance".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:141
verses.text: The more numerous my sufferings, the sweeter will be Thy mercy.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:142
verses.text: Therefore follows: "The Lord will commend His loving-kindness in the day-time; and in the night-time will He declare it".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:143
verses.text: In tribulation no man has leisure to hear: attend, when it is well with you; hear, when it is well with you; learn, when you are in tranquillity, the discipline of wisdom, and store up the word of God as you do food.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:144
verses.text: For in tribulation every one must be profited by what he heard in the time of security.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:145
verses.text: For in prosperity God "commends to thee His mercy," in case thou serve Him faithfully, for He frees thee from tribulation; but it is "in the night" only that He "declares" His mercy to thee, which He "commended" to thee by day.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:146
verses.text: When tribulation shall actually come, He will not leave thee destitute of His help; He will show thee that which He commended to thee in the daytime is true.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:147
verses.text: For it is written in a certain passage, "The mercy of the Lord is seasonable in the time of affliction, as clouds of rain in the time of drought".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:148
verses.text: "The Lord hath commended His loving-kindness in the day-time, and in the night will He declare it".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:149
verses.text: He does not show that He is thine Helper, unless tribulation come, from whence thou must be rescued by Him who promised it to thee "in the day-time".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:150
verses.text: Therefore we are warned to be like "the ant".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:151
verses.text: For just as worldly prosperity is signified by "the day," adversity by the night, so again in another way worldly prosperity is expressed by "the summer," adversity by the winter.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:152
verses.text: And what is it that the ant does? She lays up in summer what will be useful to her in winter.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:153
verses.text: Whilst therefore it is summer, whilst it is well with you, whilst you are in tranquillity, hear the word of the Lord.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:154
verses.text: For how can it be that in the midst of these tempests of the world, you should pass through the whole of that sea, without suffering? How could it happen? To what mortal's lot has it fallen? If even it has been the lot of any, that very calm is more to be dreaded.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:155
verses.text: "The Lord hath commended His loving-kindness in the day-time, and in the night-time will He declare it".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:156
verses.text: "There is with me prayer unto the God of my life".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:157
verses.text: This I make my business here; I who am the "hart thirsting and longing for the water-brooks," calling to mind the sweetness of that strain, by which I was led on through the tabernacle even to the house of God; whilst this "corruptible body presseth down the soul,"  there is yet with me "prayer unto the God of my life".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:158
verses.text: For in order to making supplication unto God, I have not to buy aught from places beyond the sea; or in order that He may hear me, have I to sail to bring from a distance frankincense and perfumes, or have I to bring "calf or ram from the flock".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:159
verses.text: There is "with me prayer to the God of my life".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:160
verses.text: I have within a victim to sacrifice; I have within an incense to place on the altar; I have within a sacrifice wherewith to propitiate my God.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:161
verses.text: "The sacrifice of God is a troubled spirit".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:162
verses.text: What sacrifice of a "troubled spirit" I have within, hear.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:163
verses.text: "I will say unto God, Thou art my lifter up.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:164
verses.text: Why hast Thou forgotten me?".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:165
verses.text: For I am suffering here, even as if Thou hadst forgotten me.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:166
verses.text: But Thou art trying me, and I know that Thou dost but put off, not take utterly from me, what Thou hast promised me.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:167
verses.text: But yet, "Why hast Thou forgotten me?" So cried our Head also, as if speaking in our name.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:168
verses.text: "My God, my God, why hast Thou forsaken me?"  I will say unto God, "Thou art my lifter up; why hast Thou forgotten me?".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:169
verses.text: "Why hast Thou rejected me?" "Rejected" me, that is to say, from that height of the apprehension of the unchangeable Truth.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:170
verses.text: "Why hast Thou rejected me?" Why, when already longing for those things, have I been cast down to these, by the weight and burden of my iniquity? This same voice in another passage said, "I said in my trance" (i-e:, in my rapture, when he had seen some great thing or other), "I said in my trance, I am cast out of the sight of Thine eyes".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:171
verses.text: For he compared these things in which he found himself, to those toward which he had been raised; and saw himself cast out far "from the sight of God's eyes," as he speaks even here, "Why hast Thou rejected me? Why go I mourning, while mine enemy troubleth me, while he breaketh my bones?" Even he, my tempter, the devil; while offences are everywhere on the increase, because of the abundance of which "the love of many is waxing cold".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:172
verses.text: When we see the strong members of the Church generally giving way to the causes of offence, does not Christ's body say, "The enemy breaketh my bones"? For it is the strong members that are "the bones;" and sometimes even those that are strong sink under their temptations.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:173
verses.text: For whosoever of the body of Christ considers this, does he not exclaim, with the voice of Christ's Body, "Why hast Thou rejected me? Why go I mourning, while mine enemy troubleth me, while he breaketh my bones?"  You may see not my flesh merely, but even my "bones".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:174
verses.text: To see those who were thought to have some stability, giving way under temptations, so that the rest of the weak brethren despair when they see those who are strong succumbing; how great, my brethren, are the dangers!.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:175
verses.text: "They who trouble me cast me in the teeth".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:176
verses.text: Again that voice! "While they say daily unto me, Where is thy God?".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:177
verses.text: And it is principally in the temptations of the Church they say this, "Where is thy God?" How much was this cast in the teeth of the Martyrs! Those men so patient and courageous for the name of Christ, how often was it said to them, "Where is your God?" "Let Him deliver you, if He can".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:178
verses.text: For men saw their torments outwardly; they did not inwardly behold their crowns! "They who trouble me cast me in the teeth, while they say daily unto me, Where is thy God?" And on this account, seeing "my soul is disquieted on account of myself," what else should I say unto it than those words:  "Why art thou cast down, O my soul; and why dost thou disquiet me?".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:179
verses.text: And, as it seems to answer, "Wouldest thou not have me disquiet thee, placed as I am here in so great evils? Wouldest thou have me not disquiet thee, panting as I am after what is good, thirsting and labouring as I am for it?" What should I say, but,  "Hope thou in God; for I will yet confess unto Him".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:180
verses.text: He states the very words of that confession; he repeats the grounds on which he fortifies his hope.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 42:181
verses.text: "He is the health of my countenance, and my God".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:1
verses.text: Psalm XLIII.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:2
verses.text: This Psalm is a short one; it satisfies the mental cravings of the hearers, without imposing too severe a trial on the hunger of those fasting Let our soul feed upon it; our soul, which he who sings in this Psalm, speaks of as "cast down;" cast down, I suppose, either in consequence of some fist, or rather in consequence of some hunger he was in.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:3
verses.text: For fasting is a voluntary act; being an-hungered is an involuntary thing.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:4
verses.text: That which is an-hungered, is the Church, is the Body of Christ: and that "Man" who is extended throughout the whole world, of which the Head is above, the limbs below: it is His voice which ought by this time to be perfectly known, and perfectly familiar, to us, in all the Psalms; now chanting joyously, now sorrowing; now rejoicing in hope, now sighing at its actual state, even as if it were our own.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:5
verses.text: We need not then dwell long on pointing out to you, who is the speaker here: let each one of us be a member of Christ's Body; and he will be speaker here.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:6
verses.text: "Judge me, O Lord, and separate my cause from the ungodly nation".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:7
verses.text: I do not dread Thy judgment, because I know Thy mercy.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:8
verses.text: "Judge me, O God," he cries.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:9
verses.text: Now, meanwhile, in this state of pilgrimage, Thou dost not yet separate my place, because I am to live together with the "tares" even to the time of the "harvest:" Thou dost not as yet separate my rain from theirs; my light from theirs: "separate my cause".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:10
verses.text: Let a difference be made between him who believes in Thee, and him who believes not in Thee.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:11
verses.text: Our infirmity is the same; but our consciences not the same: our sufferings the same; but our longings not the same.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:12
verses.text: "The desire of the ungodly shall perish," but as to the desire of the righteous, we might well doubt, if He were not "sure" who promised.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:13
verses.text: The object of our desires is He Himself, who promiseth: He will give us Himself, because He has already given Himself to us; He will give Himself in His immortality to us then immortal, even because He gave Himself in His mortality to us when mortal.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:14
verses.text: And since patience is needful in order to endure, until the harvest, a certain distinction without separation, if we may so speak (for they are together with us, and therefore not yet separated; the tares however being still tares, and the corn still corn, and therefore they are already distinct); since then a kind of strength is needful, which must be implored of Him who bids us to be strong, and without whose making us strong, we should not be what He bids us to be; of Him who said, "He that endures unto the end shall be saved," lest the soul's powers should be impaired in consequence of her ascribing any strength to herself, he subjoins immediately,  "For Thou, O God, art my strength: why hast Thou cast me off, and why go I mourning, while the enemy harasseth me?".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:15
verses.text: I go mourning: the enemy is harassing me with daily temptations: inspiring either some unlawful love, or some ungrounded cause of fear; and the soul that fights against both of them, though not taken prisoner by them, yet being in danger from them, is contracted with sorrow, and says unto God, "Why?"  Let her then ask of Him, and hear "Why?" For she is in the Psalm enquiring the cause of her dejection; saying, "Why hast Thou cast me off? and why go I mourning?" Let her hear from Isaiah; let the lesson which has just been read, suggest itself to her.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:16
verses.text: "The spirit shall go forth from me, and every breath have I made.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:17
verses.text: For iniquity have I a little afflicted him; I hid my face from him, and he departed from me sorrowful in the ways of his heart".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:18
verses.text: Why then didst thou ask, "Why hast Thou cast me off, and why go I mourning?" Thou hast heard, it was "for iniquity".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:19
verses.text: "Iniquity" is the cause of thy mourning; let "Righteousness" be the cause of thy rejoicing! Thou wouldest sin; and yet thou wouldest fain not suffer; so that it was too little for thee to be thyself unrighteous, without also wishing Him to be unrighteous, in that thou wouldest fain not be punished by Him.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:20
verses.text: Consider a speech of a better kind in another Psalm.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:21
verses.text: "It is good for me that Thou hast humbled me, that I might learn Thy righteousnesses".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:22
verses.text: By being lifted up, I had learned my own iniquities; let me by being "humbled," learn "Thy righteousnesses".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:23
verses.text: "Why go I mourning, while the enemy harasses me?" Thou complainest of the enemy.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:24
verses.text: It is true he does harass thee; but it was thou didst "give place" to him.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:25
verses.text: And even now there is a course open to thee; choose the course of prudence; admit thy King, shut the tyrant out.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:26
verses.text: But in order that she may do this, hear what she says, what she supplicates, what she prays for.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:27
verses.text: Pray thou for what thou hearest; pray for it when thou hearest it; let these words be the voice of us all: "O send out Thy Light and Thy Truth.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:28
verses.text: They have led me, and brought me on unto Thy holy hill, and into Thy Tabernacles".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:29
verses.text: For that very "Light" and "Truth" are indeed two in name; the reality expressed is but One.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:30
verses.text: For what else is the "Light" of God, except the "Truth" of God? Or what else is the "Truth" of God, except the "Light" of God? And the one Person of Christ is both of these.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:31
verses.text: "I am the Light of the world: he that believeth on Me, shall not walk in darkness".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:32
verses.text: "I am the Way, the Truth, and the Life".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:33
verses.text: He is Himself "the Light:" He is Himself "the Truth".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:34
verses.text: Let Him come then and rescue us, and "separate at once our cause from the ungodly nation; let Him deliver us from the deceitful and unjust man," let him separate the wheat from the tares, for at the time of harvest He will Himself send His Angels, that they may "gather out of His kingdom all things that offend," and cast them into flaming fire, while they gather together the corn into the garner.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:35
verses.text: He will send out His "Light," and His "Truth;" for that they have already "brought us and led us to His holy hill, and into His Tabernacles".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:36
verses.text: We possess the "earnest;" we hope for the prize.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:37
verses.text: "His holy Hill" is His holy Church.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:38
verses.text: It is that mountain which, according to Daniel's vision, grew from a very small "stone," till it crushed the kingdoms of the earth; and grew to such a size, that it "filled the face of the earth".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:39
verses.text: This is the "hill," from which he tells us that his prayer was heard, who says, "I cried unto the Lord with my voice, and He heard me out of His holy hill".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:40
verses.text: Let no one of those that are without that mountain, hope to be heard unto eternal life.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:41
verses.text: For many are heard in their prayers for many things.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:42
verses.text: Let them not congratulate themselves on being heard; the devils were heard in their prayer, that they might be sent into the swine.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:43
verses.text: Let us desire to be heard unto eternal life, by reason of our longing, through which we say, "Send out Thy Light and Thy Truth".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:44
verses.text: That is a "Light" which requires the eye of the heart.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:45
verses.text: For "Blessed" (He saith) "are the pure in heart, for they shall see God".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:46
verses.text: We are now on His Hill, that is, in His Church, and in His Tabernacle.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:47
verses.text: The "tabernacle" is for persons sojourning; the house, for those dwelling in one community The tabernacle is also for those who are both from home, and also in a state of warfare.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:48
verses.text: When thou hearest of a tabernacle, form a notion of a war; guard against an enemy.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:49
verses.text: But what shall the house be? "Blessed are they that dwell in Thine house: they will be alway praising Thee".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:50
verses.text: Now then that we have been led on even to "the Tabernacle," and are placed on "His holy Hill," what hope do we carry with us?  "Then will I go in unto the Altar of God".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:51
verses.text: For there is a certain invisible Altar on high, which the unrighteous man approaches not.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:52
verses.text: To that Altar he alone draws nigh, who draws nigh to this one without cause to fear.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:53
verses.text: There he shall find his Life, who in this one "separates his cause".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:54
verses.text: "And I will go in unto the Altar of God".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:55
verses.text: From His holy Hill, and from His Tabernacle, from His Holy Church, I will go in unto the Altar of God on High.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:56
verses.text: What manner of Sacrifice is there? He himself who goeth in is taken for a burnt-offering.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:57
verses.text: "I will go in unto the Altar of God".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:58
verses.text: What is the meaning of what he says, "The Altar of my God"?  "Unto God, who makes glad my youth".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:59
verses.text: Youth signifies newness: just as if he said, "Unto God, who makes glad my newness".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:60
verses.text: It is He who makes glad my newness, who hath filled my old estate with mourning.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:61
verses.text: For now "I go mourning" in oldness, then shall "I stand," exulting in newness!  "Yea, upon the harp will I praise Thee, O God my God".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:62
verses.text: What is the meaning of "praising on the harp," and praising on the psaltery? For he does not always do so with the harp, nor always with the psaltery.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:63
verses.text: These two instruments of the musicians have each a distinct meaning of their own, worthy of our consideration and notice.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:64
verses.text: They are both borne in the hands, and played by the touch; and they stand for certain bodily works of ours.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:65
verses.text: Both are good, if one knows how to play the psaltery, or to play the harp But since the psaltery is that instrument which has the shell (i-e: that drum, that hollow piece of wood, by straining on which the chords resound) on the upper part of it, whereas the harp has that same concave sounding-board on the lower part, there is to be a distinction made between our works, when they are "upon the harp," when "on the psaltery:" both however are acceptable to God, and grateful to His ear.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:66
verses.text: When we do anything according to God's Commandments, obeying His commands and hearkening to Him, that we may fulfil His injunctions, when we are active and not passive, it is the psaltery that is playing.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:67
verses.text: For so also do the Angels: for they have nothing to suffer.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:68
verses.text: But when we suffer anything of tribulation, of trials, of offences on this earth (as we suffer only from the inferior part of ourselves; i-e: from the fact that we are mortal, that we owe somewhat of tribulation to our original cause, and also from the fact of our suffering much from those who are not "above"); this is "the harp".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:69
verses.text: For there rises a sweet strain from that part of us which is "below:" we "suffer," and we strike the psaltery, or shall I rather say we sing and we strike the harp.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:70
verses.text: And again, in order that he may draw the sound from that sounding-board below, he addresses his soul: he says, "Why art thou sorrowful, O my soul, and why dost thou disquiet me?".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:71
verses.text: I am in tribulations, in weariness, in mourning, "Why dost thou disquiet me, O my soul?" Who is the speaker, to whom is he speaking? That it is the soul to which he is speaking, everybody knows: for it is obvious: the appeal is addressed to it directly: "Why art thou sorrowful, O my soul, and why dost thou disquiet me?" The question is as to the speaker.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:72
verses.text: It is not the flesh addressing the soul, surely, since the flesh cannot speak without the soul.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:73
verses.text: For it is more appropriate for the soul to address the flesh, than for the flesh to address the soul.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:74
verses.text: We perceive then that we have a certain part, in which is "the image of God;" viz.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:75
verses.text: the mind and reason It was that same mind that prayed for "God's Light" and "God's Truth".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:76
verses.text: It is the same mind by which we apprehend right and wrong: it is by the same that we discern truth from falsehood.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:77
verses.text: It is this same that we call "understanding;" which "understanding," indeed, is wanting to the brutes.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:78
verses.text: And this "understanding" whoever neglects in himself, and holds it in less account than the other parts of his nature, and casts it off, just as if he had it not, is addressed in the Psalm, "Be ye not as the horse and the mule, which have no understanding".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:79
verses.text: It is our "understanding" then that is addressing our soul.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:80
verses.text: The latter is withered away from tribulations, worn out in anguish, made "sorrowful" in temptations, fainting in toils.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:81
verses.text: The mind, catching a glimpse of Truth above, would fain rouse her spirits, and she says, "Why art thou sorrowful, O my soul?".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:82
verses.text: These expressions, brethren, are safe ones: but yet be watchful in good works.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:83
verses.text: Touch "the psaltery," by obeying the Commandments; touch the harp, by patiently enduring your sufferings.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:84
verses.text: You have heard from Isaiah, "Break thy bread to the hungry;" think not that fasting by itself is sufficient.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:85
verses.text: Fasting chasteneth thine own self: it does not refresh others.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:86
verses.text: Thy distress will profit thee, if thou affordest comfort to others.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:87
verses.text: See, thou hast denied thyself; to whom wilt thou give that of which thou hast deprived thyself? Where wilt thou bestow what thou hast denied thyself? How many poor may be filled by the breakfast we have this day given up? Fast in such a way that thou mayest rejoice, that thou hast breakfasted, while another has been eating; fast on account of thy prayers, that thou mayest be heard in them.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:88
verses.text: For He says in that passage, "Whilst thou art yet speaking I will say, Here I am," provided thou wilt with cheerful mind "break thy bread to the hungry".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:89
verses.text: For generally this is done by men reluctantly and with murmurs, to rid themselves of the wearisome importunity of the beggar, not to refresh the bowels of him that is needy.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:90
verses.text: But it is "a cheerful giver" that "God loves".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:91
verses.text: If thou givest thy bread reluctantly, thou hast lost both the bread, and the merit of the action.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:92
verses.text: Do it then from the heart: that He "who seeth in secret," may say, "whilst thou art yet speaking, Here I am".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:93
verses.text: How speedily are the prayers of those received, who work righteousness! And this is man's righteousness in this life, fasting, alms, and prayer.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:94
verses.text: Wouldest thou have thy prayer fly upward to God? Make for it those two wings of alms and fasting.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 43:95
verses.text: Such may God's "Light" and God's "Truth" find us, that He may find us without cause for fear, when He comes to free us from death, who has already come to undergo death for us, Amen.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 44:1
verses.text: Psalm XLIV.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 44:2
verses.text: This Psalm is addressed "to the sons of Korah," as its title shows.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 44:3
verses.text: Now Korah is equivalent to the word baldness; and we find in the Gospel that ou r Lord Jesus Christ was crucified in "the place of a skull".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 44:4
verses.text: It is clear then that this Psalm is sung to the "sons of His 'Passion.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 44:5
verses.text: '" Now we have on this point a most certain and most evident testimony from the Apostle Paul; because that at the time when the Church was suffering under the persecutions of the Gentiles, he quoted from hence a verse, to insert by way of consolation, and encouragement to patience.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 44:6
verses.text: For that which he inserted in his Epistle, is said here: "For Thy sake are we kille d all the day long; we are counted as sheep for the slaughter".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 44:7
verses.text: Let us then hear in this Psalm the voice of the Martyrs; and see how good is the cause which the voice of the Martyrs pleads, saying, For Thy sake, etc.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 44:8
verses.text: The title then is not simply "To the sons of Korah," but, "For understanding, to the sons of Korah".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 44:9
verses.text: This is the case also with that Psalm, the first verse of which the Lord Himself uttered on the Cross: "My God, My God, look upon Me; why hast Thou forsaken Me?" For "transferring us in a figure" to what He was saying, and to His own Body (for we are also "His Body," and He is our "Head"), He uttered from the Cross not His own cry, but ours.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 44:10
verses.text: For God never "forsook" Him: nor did He Himself ever depart from the Father; but it was in behalf of us that He spake this: "My God, My God, why hast thou forsaken Me?" For there follows, "Far from My health are the words of My offences:" and it shows in whose person He said this; for sin could not be found in Him.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 44:11
verses.text: "O God, we have heard with our ears; our fathers have told us the work that Thou didst in their days, and in the days of old".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 44:12
verses.text: Wondering wherefore, in these days, He has seemingly forsaken those whom it was His will to exercise in sufferings, they recall the past events which they have heard of from their fathers; as if they said,  It is not of these things that we suffer, that our fathers told us! For in that other Psalm also, He said this, "Our fathers trusted in Thee; they trusted, and Thou didst deliver them.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 44:13
verses.text: But I am a worm and no man; a reproach of men, and the outcast of the people".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 44:14
verses.text: They trusted, and Thou didst deliver them; have I then hoped, and hast Thou forsaken me? And have I believed upon Thee in vain? And is it in vain that my name has been written in Thy Book, and Thy name has been inscribed on me? What our fathers told us was this:  "Thy hand destroyed the nations; and Thou plantedst them: Thou didst weaken the peoples, and cast them out".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 44:15
verses.text: That is to say: "Thou didst drive out 'the peoples' from their own land, that Thou mightest bring 'them' in, and plant them; and mightest by Thy mercy stablish their kingdom".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 44:16
verses.text: These are the things that we heard from our fathers.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 44:17
verses.text: But perhaps it was because they were brave, were men of battle, were invincible, were well-disciplined, and warlike, that they could do these things.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 44:18
verses.text: Far from it.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 44:19
verses.text: This is not what our fathers told us; this is not what is contained in Scripture.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 44:20
verses.text: But what does it say, but what follows?  "For they gat not the land in possession by their own sword, neither did their own arm save them; but Thy right hand, and Thine arm, and the light of Thy countenance".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 44:21
verses.text: Thy "right hand" is Thy Power: Thine "arm" is Thy Son Himself And "the light of Thy countenance".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 44:22
verses.text: What means this, but that Thou wert present with them, in miracles of such a sort that Thy presence was perceived.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 44:23
verses.text: For when God's presence with us appears by any miracle, do we see His face with our own eyes? No.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 44:24
verses.text: It is by the effect of the miracle He intimates to man His presence.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 44:25
verses.text: In fact, what do all persons say, who express wonder at facts of this description? "I saw God present".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 44:26
verses.text: "But Thy right hand, and Thine arm, and the light of Thy countenance; because Thou pleasedst in them:" i-e: didst so deal with them, that Thou wert well-pleasing in them: that whoso considered how they were being dealt with, might say, that "God is with them of a truth;" and it is God that moves them.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 44:27
verses.text: "What? Was He then other than now He is?" Away with the supposition.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 44:28
verses.text: For what follows?  "Thou art Thyself my King and my God".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 44:29
verses.text: "Thou art Thyself;" for Thou art not changed.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 44:30
verses.text: I see that the times are changed; but the Creator of times is unchanged.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 44:31
verses.text: "Thou art Thyself my King and my God".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 44:32
verses.text: Thou art wont to guide me: to govern me, to save me.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 44:33
verses.text: "Thou who commandest salvation unto Jacob".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 44:34
verses.text: What is, "Thou who commandest"? Even though in Thine own proper Substance and Nature, in which Thou art whatsoever Thou art, Thou wast hid from them; and though Thou didst not converse with the fathers in that which Thou art in Thyself, so that they could see Thee "face to face," yet by any created being whatsoever "Thou commandest salvation unto Israel".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 44:35
verses.text: For that sight of Thee "face to face" is reserved for those set free in the Resurrection.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 44:36
verses.text: And the very "fathers" of the New Testament too, although they saw Thy mysteries revealed, although they preached the secret things so revealed to them, nevertheless said that they themselves saw but "in a glass, darkly," but that "seeing face to face"  is reserved to a future time, when what the Apostle himself speaks of shall have come.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 44:37
verses.text: "When Christ our life shall appear, then shall ye also appear with Him in glory".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 44:38
verses.text: It is against that time then that vision "face to face" is reserved for you, of which John also speaks: "Beloved, we are now the sons of God: and it doth not yet appear what we shall be.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 44:39
verses.text: We know that, when He shall appear, we shall be like Him; for we shall see Him as He is".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 44:40
verses.text: Although then at that time our fathers saw Thee not as Thou art, "face to face," although that vision is reserved against the resurrection, yet, even though they were Angels who presented themselves, it is Thou, "Who commandest salvation unto Jacob".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 44:41
verses.text: Thou art not only present by Thine own Self; but by whatsoever created being Thou didst appear, it is Thou that dost "command" by them, that which Thou doest by Thine own Self in order to the salvation of Thy servants: but that which they do whom Thou "commandest" it, is done to procure the salvation of Thy servants.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 44:42
verses.text: Since then Thou art Thyself "my King and my God, and Thou commandest salvation unto Jacob," wherefore are we suffering these things?.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 44:43
verses.text: But perhaps it is only what is past that has been described to us: but nothing of the kind is to be hoped for by us for the future.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 44:44
verses.text: Nay indeed, it is still to be hoped for.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 44:45
verses.text: "Through Thee will we winnow away our enemies".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 44:46
verses.text: Our fathers then have declared to us a work that Thou didst "in their days, and in the days of old," that Thy hand destroyed the Gentiles: that Thou "didst cast out the peoples; and didst plant them".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 44:47
verses.text: Such was the past; but what is to be hereafter? "Through Thee we shall winnow away our enemies".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 44:48
verses.text: A time will come, when all the enemies of Christians will be winnowed away like chaff, be blown like dust, and be cast off from the earth.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 44:49
