verses.text: Thou sayest true: God hath promised pardon to thy conversion; He hath not promised a to-morrow to thy delay.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:68
verses.text: "Sweet is the Lord to all, and His compassions are over all His works".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:69
verses.text: Why then doth He condemn? why doth He scourge? Are not they whom He condemneth, whom He scourgeth, His works? Plainly they are.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:70
verses.text: And wilt thou know how "His compassions are over all His works"? Thence is that long-suffering, whereby "He maketh His sun to rise on the evil and on the good".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:71
verses.text: Are not "His compassions over all His works, who sendeth rain upon the just and upon the unjust"? In His long-suffering He waiteth for the sinner, saying, "Turn ye to Me, and I will turn to you".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:72
verses.text: Are not "His compassions over all His works"? And when He saith, "Go ye into everlasting fire, prepared for the devil and his angels," this is not His compassion, but His severity.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:73
verses.text: His compassion is given to His works: His severity is not over His works, but over thy works.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:74
verses.text: Lastly, if thou remove thine own evil works, and there remain in thee nought but His work, His compassion will not leave thee: but if thou leavest not thy works, there will be severity over thy works, not over His works.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:75
verses.text: "Let all Thy works, O Lord, confess to Thee, and let Thy saints bless Thee".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:76
verses.text: How so? Is not the earth His work? Are not the trees His work? Cattle, beasts, fish, fowl, are not they His works? Plainly they too are.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:77
verses.text: And how shall these too confess to Him? I see indeed in the angels that His works confess to Him, for the angels are His works: and men are His works; and when men confess to Him, His works confess to Him; but have trees and stones the voice of confession? Yes, verily; "let all" His "works confess to" Him.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:78
verses.text: What sayest thou? even the earth and the trees?But there ariseth the same question in regard of praise, as in regard of confession.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:79
verses.text: For if earth and all things devoid of sensation therefore cannot confess, because they have no voice to confess with; neither will they be able to praise, because they have no voice to proclaim with.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:80
verses.text: But do not those Three Children enumerate all things, as they walked amid the harmless flames, who had leisure not only not to fear, but even to praise God? They say to all things, heavenly and earthly, "Bless ye the Lord, praise Him and magnify Him for ever".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:81
verses.text: Behold how they praise.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:82
verses.text: Let none think that the dumb stone or dumb animal hath reason wherewith to comprehend God.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:83
verses.text: They who have thought this, have erred far from the truth.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:84
verses.text: God hath ordered everything, and made everything: to some He hath given sense and understanding and immortality, as to the angels; to some He hath given sense and understanding with mortality, as to man; to some He hath given bodily sense, yet gave them not understanding, or immortality, as to cattle: to some He hath given neither sense, nor understanding, nor immortality, as to herbs, trees, stones: yet even these cannot be wanting in their kind, and by certain degrees He hath ordered His creation, from earth up to heaven, from visible to invisible, from mortal to immortal.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:85
verses.text: This framework of creation, this most perfectly ordered beauty, ascending from lowest to highest, descending from highest to lowest, never broken, but tempered together of things unlike, all praiseth God.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:86
verses.text: Wherefore then doth all praise God? Because when thou considerest it, and seest its beauty, thou in it praisest God.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:87
verses.text: The beauty of the earth is a kind of voice of the dumb earth.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:88
verses.text: And this which thou hast found in it, is the very voice of its confession, that thou praise the Creator.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:89
verses.text: When thou hast thought on the universal beauty of this world, doth not its very beauty as it were with one voice answer thee, "I made not myself, God made me"?.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:90
verses.text: For when Thy saints bless Thee, what say they? "They shall tell the glory of Thy kingdom, and talk of Thy Power".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:91
verses.text: How powerful is God, who hath made the earth! how powerful is God, who hath filled the earth with good things! how powerful is God, who hath given to the animals each its own life! how powerful is God, who hath given different seeds to the womb of the earth, that they might make to spring up such various shoots, such beautiful trees! how powerful, how great is God! Do thou ask, creation answereth, and by its answer, as by the confession of the creature, thou, O saint of God, blessest God, and "talkest of His power".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:92
verses.text: "That they may make known to the sons of men Thy power, and the glory of the greatness of the beauty of Thy kingdom".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:93
verses.text: Thy saints then commend "the glory of the greatness of the beauty of Thy kingdom," the glory of the greatness of its beauty.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:94
verses.text: There is a certain "greatness of the beauty of Thy kingdom:" that is, Thy kingdom hath beauty, and great beauty.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:95
verses.text: Since whatever hath beauty, hath beauty from Thee, how great beauty hath Thy whole kingdom! Let not the kingdom frighten us: it hath beauty also, wherewith to delight us.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:96
verses.text: For what is that beauty, which the saints shall hereafter enjoy, to whom it shall be said, "Come, ye blessed of My Father, enjoy the kingdom"? Whence shall they come? whither shall they come? Behold, brethren, and, if ye can, as far as ye can, think of the beauty of that kingdom which is to come; whence our prayer saith, "Thy kingdom come".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:97
verses.text: For that kingdom we desire may come, that kingdom the saints proclaim to be coming.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:98
verses.text: Observe this world: it is beautiful.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:99
verses.text: How beautiful are earth, sea, air, heavens, stars.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:100
verses.text: Do not all these frighten him who considereth them? Is not the beauty of them so conspicuous, that it seemeth as though nothing more beautiful could be found? And here, in this beauty, in this fairness almost unspeakable, here worm and mice and all creeping things of the earth live with thee, they live with thee in all this beauty.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:101
verses.text: How great is the beauty of that kingdom where none but angels live with Thee! There is a greatness of a certain beauty; let it be loved before it is seen, that when it is seen, it may be retained.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:102
verses.text: "Thy kingdom".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:103
verses.text: What kingdom mean I? "a kingdom of all ages".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:104
verses.text: For the kingdom of this age too hath its own beauty, but there is not in it that greatness of beauty, such as in the "kingdom of all ages".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:105
verses.text: "And Thy dominion is in every generation and generation".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:106
verses.text: This is the repetition we noticed, signifying either every generation, or the generation which will be after this generation.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:107
verses.text: "Faithful is the Lord in His words, and holy in all His works".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:108
verses.text: "Faithful is the Lord in His words:" for what hath He promised that He hath not given? "Faithful is the Lord in His words".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:109
verses.text: Hereto there are certain things which He hath promised, and hath not given; but let Him be believed from the things which He hath given.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:110
verses.text: We might well believe Him, if He only spake: He willed not that we should believe Him speaking, but that we should have His Scriptures in our hands:as though a kind of bond of God's, which all who pass by might read, and might keep to the path of its promise.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:111
verses.text: And how great things hath He already paid in accordance with that bond! Do men hesitate to believe Him concerning the Resurrection of the dead and the Life to come, which alone now remaineth to be paid, when, if He come to reckon with the unbelievers, the unbelievers must blush? If God say to thee, "Thou hast My bond: I have promised judgment, the separation of good and bad, everlasting life for the faithful, and wilt thou not believe? There in My bond read all that I have promised, reckon with me: verily even by counting up what I have paid, thou canst believe that I shall pay what still I owe.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:112
verses.text: In that bond thou hast My only-begotten Son promised, "Whom I spared not, but gave Him up for you all:" reckon this then among what is paid.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:113
verses.text: Read the bond: I promised therein that I would give by My Son the earnest of the Holy Spirit: reckon that as paid.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:114
verses.text: I promised therein the blood and the crowns of the glorious Martyrs; let the White Mass remind you that My debt has been paid.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:115
verses.text: He setteth before the eyes of all His payment of His debts: some He hath paid in the time of our ancestors, which we saw not: some He hath paid in our times, which they saw not; throughout all generations He hath paid what was written.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:116
verses.text: And what remaineth? Do men not believe Him, when He hath paid all this? What remaineth? Behold thou hast reckoned: all this He hath paid: is He become unfaithful for the few things which remain? God forbid! Wherefore? Because "the Lord is faithful in His words, and holy in all His works".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:117
verses.text: "The Lord strengtheneth all that are falling".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:118
verses.text: But who are "all that are falling"? All indeed fall in a general sense, but he meaneth those who fall in a particular way.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:119
verses.text: For many fall from Him, many also fall from their own imaginations.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:120
verses.text: If they had evil imaginations, they fall from them, and "God strengthened all that are falling".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:121
verses.text: They who lose anything in this world, yet are holy, are as it were dishonoured in this world, from rich become poor, from honoured of low estate, yet are they God's saints; they are, as it were, falling.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:122
verses.text: But "God strengtheneth".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:123
verses.text: For "the just falleth seven times, and riseth again; but the wicked shall be weakened in evils".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:124
verses.text: When evils befall the wicked, they are weakened thereby; when evils befall the righteous, "the Lord strengtheneth all that are falling".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:125
verses.text: "And lifteth up all those that have been cast down:" all, that is, who belong to him; for "God resisteth the proud".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:126
verses.text: "The eyes of all hope upon Thee, and Thou givest them food in due season".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:127
verses.text: Just as when thou refreshest a sick man in due season, when he ought to receive, then Thou givest, and what he ought to receive, that Thou givest.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:128
verses.text: Sometimes then men long, and he giveth not: he who tendeth, knoweth the time to give.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:129
verses.text: Wherefore say I this, brethren? Lest any one be faint, if perchance he hath not been heard, when making some righteous request of God.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:130
verses.text: For when he maketh any unrighteous request, he is heard to his punishment: but when making some righteous request of God, if perchance he have not been heard, let him not be down-hearted, let him not faint, let his eyes wait for the food, which He giveth in due season.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:131
verses.text: When He giveth not, He therefore giveth not, lest that which He giveth do harm"Thou givest them meat in due season".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:132
verses.text: "Thou openest Thine Hand, and fillest every living thing with blessing".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:133
verses.text: Though sometimes Thou givest not, yet "in due season" Thou givest: Thou delayest, not deniest, and that in due season".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:134
verses.text: "Righteous is the Lord in all His ways, and holy in all His works".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:135
verses.text: Both when He smiteth and when He healeth, He is righteous, and in Him unrighteousness is not.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:136
verses.text: Finally, all His saints, when set in the midst of tribulation, have first praised His righteousness, and so sought His blessings.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:137
verses.text: They first have said, "What Thou doest is righteous".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:138
verses.text: So did Daniel ask, and other holy men: "Righteous are Thy judgments: rightly have we suffered: deservedly have we suffered".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:139
verses.text: They laid not unrighteousness to God, they laid not to Him injustice and folly.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:140
verses.text: First they praised Him scourging, and so they felt Him feeding.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:141
verses.text: "The Lord is nigh unto all that call upon Him".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:142
verses.text: Where then is that, "Then shall they call upon Me, and I will not hear them"? See then what follows: "all who call upon Him in truth".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:143
verses.text: For many call upon Him, but not in truth.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:144
verses.text: They seek something else from Him, but seek not Himself.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:145
verses.text: Why lovest thou God? "Because He hath made me whole".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:146
verses.text: That is clear: it was He that made thee so.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:147
verses.text: For from none else cometh health, save Him.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:148
verses.text: "Because He gave me," saith another, "a rich wife, whereas I before had nothing, and one that obeyeth me".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:149
verses.text: This too He gave: thou sayest true.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:150
verses.text: "He gave me," saith another, "sons many and good, He gave me a household, He gave me all good things".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:151
verses.text: Dost thou love Him for this?Therefore if God is good, who hath given thee what thou hast, how much more blessed wilt thou be when He hath given thee Himself! Thou hast desired all these things of Him: I beseech thee desire of Him Himself also.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:152
verses.text: For these things are not truly sweeter than He is, nor in any way are they to be compared to Him.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:153
verses.text: He then who preferreth God Himself to all the things which he has received, whereat he rejoiceth, to the things he has received, he "calleth upon God in truth".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:154
verses.text: "He will perform the will of them that fear Him".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:155
verses.text: He will perform it, He will perform it: though He perform it not at once, yet He will perform it.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:156
verses.text: Certainly if therefore thou fearest God, that thou mayest do His will, behold even He in a manner ministereth to thee; He doeth thy will.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:157
verses.text: "And He shall hear their prayer, and save them".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:158
verses.text: Thou seest that for this purpose the Physician hears, that He may save.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:159
verses.text: When? Hear the Apostle telling thee.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:160
verses.text: "For we are saved in hope: but hope which is seen is not hope: but if what we see not we hope for, then do we with patience wait for it: "the salvation," that is, which Peter calleth "ready to be revealed in the last time".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:161
verses.text: "The Lord guardeth all that love Him, and all sinners He will destroy".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:162
verses.text: Thou seest that there is severity with Him, with whom is so great sweetness.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:163
verses.text: He will save all that hope in Him, all the faithful, all that fear Him, all that call upon Him in truth: "and all sinners He will destroy".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:164
verses.text: What "all sinners," save those who persevere in sin; who dare to blame God, not themselves; who daily argue against God; who despair of pardon for their sins, and from this very despair heap up their sins; or who perversely promise themselves pardon, and through this very promise depart not from their sins and impiety? The time will come for all these to be separated, and for the two divisions to be made of them, one on the right hand, the other on the left; and for the righteous to receive the everlasting Kingdom, the wicked to go into everlasting fire.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 145:165
verses.text: Since this is so, and we have heard the blessing of the Lord, the works of the Lord, the wondrous things of the Lord, the mercies of the Lord, the severity of the Lord, His Providence over all His works, the confession of all His works; observe how He concludeth in His praise, "My mouth shall speak the praise of the Lord, and let all flesh bless His holy Name for ever and ever".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:1
verses.text: Psalm CXLVI.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:2
verses.text: Behold the Psalm soundeth; it is the voice of some one (and that some one are ye, if ye will), of some one encouraging his soul to praise God, and saying to himself, "Praise the Lord, O my soul".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:3
verses.text: For sometimes in the tribulations and temptations of this present life, wh ether we will or no, our soul is troubled; of which troubling he speaketh in another Psalm But to remove this troubling, he suggesteth joy; not as yet in reality, but in hope; and saith to it when troubled and anxious, sad and sorrowing, "Hope in God, for I will yet confess to Him".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:4
verses.text: But who saith it, and to whom saith he it? What shall we say, brethren? Is it the flesh that saith, "Praise thou the Lord, O my soul"? And can the flesh suggest good counsel to the soul? However much the flesh be conquered, and subjected as a servant to us through strength which the Lord imparteth, that it serve us entirely as a bond slave, enough for us that it hinder us not.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:5
verses.text: For the body, inasmuch as it is the body, is even beneath the soul; and every soul, however vile, is found more excellent than the most excellent body.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:6
verses.text: And let not this seem to you to be wonderful, that even any vile and sinful soul is better than any great and most surpassing body.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:7
verses.text: It is better, not in deserts, but in nature.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:8
verses.text: The soul indeed is sinful, is stained with certain defilements of lusts; yet gold, though rusted, is better than the most polished lead.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:9
verses.text: Let your mind then run over every part of creation, and ye will see that what we are saying is not incredible, that a soul, however blameable, is yet more praiseworthy than a praiseworthy body.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:10
verses.text: There are two things, a soul and a body.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:11
verses.text: The soul I chide, the body I praise: the soul I chide, because it is sinful; the body I praise, because it is sound.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:12
verses.text: Yet it is in its own kind that I praise the soul, and in its own kind that I blame the soul: and so in its own kind I praise the body, or blame it.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:13
verses.text: If you ask me which is better, what I have blamed or what I have praised, wondrous is the answer thou wilt receive.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:14
verses.text: So you speak of the best horse and the worst man: yet thou preferrest the man thou findest fault with to the horse thou praisest.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:15
verses.text: The nature of the soul is more excellent than the nature of the body: it surpasseth it by far, it is a thing spiritual, incorporeal, akin to the substance of God.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:16
verses.text: It is somewhat invisible, it ruleth the body, moveth the limbs, guideth the senses, prepareth thoughts, putteth forth actions, taketh in images of countless things; who is there, in short, beloved brethren, who may suffice for the praises of the soul? And yet such is the grace given to it, that this man saith, "Praise the Lord, O my soul".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:17
verses.text: It is not the flesh that saith it.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:18
verses.text: Let the body be angel-like, still it is inferior to the soul, it cannot give advice to its superior.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:19
verses.text: The flesh when duly obedient is the handmaid of the soul: the soul rules, the body obeys; the soul commands, the body performs; how then can the flesh give this advice to the soul? Is it then perchance the soul herself, who saith to herself, and in a manner commandeth herself, and exhorteth and asketh herself? For through certain passions in one part of her nature she wavered; but in another part, which they call the reasonable mind, the wisdom whereby she thinks, clinging to God, and now sighing towards Him, she perceives that certain inferior parts of her are troubled by worldly emotions, and by a certain excitement of earthly desires, betake them to outward things, leaving God who is within; so she recalleth herself from things outward to inward, from lower to higher, and says, "Praise the Lord, O my soul".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:20
verses.text: The soul itself giveth itself counsel from the light of God by the reasonable mind, whereby it conceiveth the wisdom fixed in the everlasting nature of its Author.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:21
verses.text: It readeth there of somewhat to be feared, to be praised, to be loved, to be longed for, and sought after: as yet it graspeth it not, it comprehendeth it not; it is, as it were, dazzled with brightness; it has not strength to abide there.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:22
verses.text: Therefore it gathers itself, as it were, into a sound state, and saith, "Praise the Lord, O my soul".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:23
verses.text: And then the soul, weighed down, as it were, and unable to stand up as is fitting, answereth the mind, "I will praise the Lord in my life".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:24
verses.text: What is, "in my life"? Because now I am in my death.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:25
verses.text: Therefore first encourage thyself, and say, "Praise the Lord, O my soul".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:26
verses.text: Thy soul answereth thee, I do praise so far as I can, slightly, poorly, weakly.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:27
verses.text: Wherefore? Because, "while we are in the body, we are absent from the Lord".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:28
verses.text: "In my life".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:29
verses.text: Now what has it? It might answer thee, "My death".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:30
verses.text: Whence, "My death"? because I am absent from the Lord.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:31
verses.text: For if to cling to Him is life, to depart from Him is death.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:32
verses.text: But what comforteth thee? Hope.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:33
verses.text: Now thou livest in hope: in hope praise, in hope sing.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:34
verses.text: Thy death is from the sadness of this life, thou livest in hope of a future life.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:35
verses.text: And how wilt thou praise thy Lord? "I will sing unto my God, as long as I have my being".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:36
verses.text: What sort of praise is this, "I will sing unto my God as long as I have being"? Behold, my brethren, what sort of being this will be; where there will be everlasting praise, there will be also everlasting being.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:37
verses.text: Behold, now thou hast being: dost thou sing unto God as long as thou hast being? Behold, thou wast singing, and hast turned thyself away to some business, thou singest no longer, yet thou hast being: thou hast being, yet thou singest not.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:38
verses.text: It may be also thy desire turneth thee to somewhat; not only dost thou not sing, but thou even offendest His ears, yet thou hast being.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:39
verses.text: What praise will that be, when thou praisest as long as thou hast being? But what meaneth, "as long as I have being"? Will there be any time when he will not be? Nay, rather, that "long" will be everlasting, and therefore it will be truly "long".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:40
verses.text: For whatever hath end in time, however prolonged it is, is yet not "long".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:41
verses.text: "Put not your trust in princes".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:42
verses.text: Brethren, here we receive a mighty task; it is a voice from heaven, from above it soundeth to us.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:43
verses.text: For now through some kind of weakness the soul of man, whensoever it is in tribulation here, despaireth of God, and chooseth to rely on man.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:44
verses.text: Let it be said to one when set in some affliction, "There is a great man, by whom thou mayest be set free;" he smileth, he rejoiceth, he is lifted up.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:45
verses.text: But if it is said to him, "God freeth thee," he is chilled, so to speak, by despair.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:46
verses.text: The aid of a mortal is promised, and thou rejoicest; the aid of the Immortal is promised, and art thou sad? It is promised thee that thou shalt be freed by one who needeth to be freed with thee, and thou exultest, as at some great aid: thou art promised that Liberator, who needeth none to free Him, and thou despairest, as though it were but a fable.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:47
verses.text: Woe to such thoughts: they wander far; truly there is sad and great death in them.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:48
verses.text: Approach, begin to long, begin to seek and to know Him by whom thou wast made.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:49
verses.text: For He will not leave His work, if He be not left by His work.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:50
verses.text: "His breath shall go forth, and he shall return to his earth: in that day shall all his thoughts perish".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:51
verses.text: Where is swelling? where is pride? where is boasting? But perhaps he will have passed to a good place, if indeed he have passed.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:52
verses.text: For I know not whither he who spake thus hath passed.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:53
verses.text: For he spake in pride; and I know not whither such men pass, save that I look into another Psalm, and see that their passage is an evil one.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:54
verses.text: "I beheld the wicked lifted up above the cedars of Libanus, and I passed by, and, lo, he was not; and I sought him, and his place was not found".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:55
verses.text: The good man, who passed by, and found not the wicked, reached a place where the wicked is not.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:56
verses.text: Wherefore, brethren, let us all listen: brethren, beloved of God, let us all listen; in whatsoever tribulation, in whatsoever longing for the heavenly gift, "let us not trust in princes, nor in sons of men, in whom is no salvation".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:57
verses.text: All this is mortal, fleeting, perishable.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:58
verses.text: What then must we do, if we are not to hope in sons of men, nor in princes? What must we do? "Blessed is he whose Helper is the God of Jacob" : not this man or that man; not this angel or that angel; but, "blessed is he whose Helper is the God of Jacob:" for to Jacob also so great an Helper was He, that of Jacob He made him Israel.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:59
verses.text: O mighty help! now he is Israel, "seeing God".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:60
verses.text: While then thou art placed here, and a wanderer not yet seeing God, if thou hast the God of Jacob for thy Helper, from Jacob thou wilt become Israel, and wilt be "seeing God," and all toil and all groans shall come to an end, gnawing cares shall cease, happy praises shall succeed.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:61
verses.text: "Blessed is he whose Helper is the God of Jacob;" of this Jacob.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:62
verses.text: Wherefore is he happy? Meanwhile, while yet groaning in this life, "his hope is in the Lord his God".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:63
verses.text: Who is this, "Lord his God"?"To us there is one God, the Father, of whom are all things, and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:64
verses.text: Therefore let Him be thy hope, even the Lord thy God; in Him let thy hope be.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:65
verses.text: His hope too is in the lord his god, who worshippeth Saturn; his hope is in the lord his god, who worshippeth Neptune or Mercury; yea more, I add, who worshippeth his belly, of whom is said, "whose god is their belly".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:66
verses.text: The one is the god of the one, the other of the other.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:67
verses.text: Who is this "blessed" one? for "his hope is in the Lord his God".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:68
verses.text: But who is He? "Who made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:69
verses.text: My brethren, we have a great God; let us bless His holy Name, that He hath deigned to make us His possession.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:70
verses.text: As yet thou seest not God; thou canst not fully love what as yet thou seest not.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:71
verses.text: All that thou seest, He hath made.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:72
verses.text: Thou admirest the world; why not the Maker of the world? Thou lookest up to the heavens, and art amazed: thou considerest the whole earth, and tremblest; when canst thou contain in thy thought the vastness of the sea? Look at the countless number of the stars, look at all the many kind of seeds, all the different sorts of animals, all that swimmeth in the water, creepeth on the earth, flieth in the sky, hovereth in the air; how great are all these, how beautiful, how fair, how amazing! Behold, He who made all these, is thy God.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:73
verses.text: Put thy hope in Him, that thou mayest be happy.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:74
verses.text: "His hope is in the Lord his God".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:75
verses.text: Observe, my brethren, the mighty God, the good God, who maketh all these things.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:76
verses.text: If he mentioned these things only, perhaps thou wouldest answer me, "God, who made heaven and earth and sea, is a great God: but doth He think of me?" It would be said to thee, "He made thee".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:77
verses.text: How so? am I heaven, or am I earth, or am I sea? Surely it is plain; I am neither heaven, nor earth, nor sea: yet I am on earth.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:78
verses.text: At least thou grantest me this, that thou art on earth.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:79
verses.text: Hear then, that God made not only heaven and earth and sea: for He "made heaven and earth and sea, and all that is in them".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:80
verses.text: If then He made all that is in them, He made thee also.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:81
verses.text: It is too little to say, thee; the sparrow, the locust, the worm, none of these did He not make, and He careth for all.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:82
verses.text: His care refers not to His commandment, for this commandment He gave to man alone.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:83
verses.text: As regards then the tenor of the commandment, "God doth not take care for oxen:" as regards His providential care of the universe, whereby He created all things, and ruleth the world, "Thou, Lord, shalt save both man and beast".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:84
verses.text: Here perhaps some one may say to me, "God careth not for oxen," comes from the New Testament: "Thou, Lord, shalt save both man and beast," is from the Old Testament.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:85
verses.text: There are some who find fault and say, that these two Testaments agree not with one another.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:86
verses.text: Let us hear the Lord Himself, the Chief and Master of the Apostles: "Consider," saith He, "the fowls of the air; they sow not, neither do they reap, nor gather into barns, and your heavenly Father feedeth them".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:87
verses.text: Therefore even beside men, these animals are objects of care to God, to be fed, not to receive a law.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:88
verses.text: As far then as regards giving a law, "God careth not for oxen:" as regards creating, feeding, governing, ruling, all things have to do with God.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:89
verses.text: "Are not two sparrows sold for one farthing?" saith our Lord Jesus Christ, "and one of them shall not fall to the ground without the will of your Father: how much better are ye than they".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:90
verses.text: Perhaps thou sayest, God counteth me not in this great multitude.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:91
verses.text: There follows here a wondrous passage in the Gospel: "the hairs of your head are all numbered".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:92
verses.text: "Who keepeth truth for ever".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:93
verses.text: What "truth for ever"? what "truth" doth He "keep," and wherein doth "He keep it for ever"? "Who executeth judgment for them that suffer wrong".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:94
verses.text: He avengeth them that suffer wrong.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:95
verses.text: There cometh at once to thee the voice of the Apostle: "now therefore there is altogether a fault among you, that ye go to law one with another: why do ye not rather suffer wrong?"  He urged thee not to suffer annoyance, but to suffer wrong: for not every annoyance is wrong.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:96
verses.text: For whatever thou sufferest lawfully is not a wrong; lest perchance thou shouldest say, I also am among those who have suffered wrong, for I have suffered such a thing in such a place, and such a thing for such a reason.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:97
verses.text: Consider whether thou hast suffered a wrong.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:98
verses.text: Robbers suffer many things, but they suffer no wrong.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:99
verses.text: Wicked men, evil doers, house-breakers, adulterers, seducers, all these suffer many evils, yet is there no wrong.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:100
verses.text: It is one thing to suffer wrong; it is another to suffer tribulation, or penalty, or annoyance, or punishment.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:101
verses.text: Consider where thou art; see what thou hast done; see why thou art suffering; and then thou seest what thou art suffering.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:102
verses.text: Right and wrong are contraries.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:103
verses.text: Right is what is just.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:104
verses.text: For not all that is called right, is right.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:105
verses.text: What if a man lay down for you unjust right? nor indeed is it to be called right, if it is unjust.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:106
verses.text: That is true right, which is also just.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:107
verses.text: Consider what thou hast done, not what thou art suffering.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:108
verses.text: If thou hast done right, thou art suffering wrong; if thou hast done wrong, thou art suffering right.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:109
verses.text: "Who giveth food to the hungry".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:110
verses.text: Behold, from thee I look for nothing: "God giveth food to the hungry".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:111
verses.text: Who are "the hungry"? All.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:112
verses.text: What is, all? To all things that have life, to all men He giveth food: doth He not reserve some food for His beloved? If they have another kind of hunger, they have also another kind of food.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:113
verses.text: Let us first enquire what their hunger is, and then we shall find their food.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:114
verses.text: "Blessed are they that hunger and thirst after righteousness, for they shall be filled".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:115
verses.text: We ought to be God's hungry ones.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:116
verses.text: "The Lord looseth them that are fettered; the Lord lifteth up them that are dashed down; the Lord maketh wise them that are blind".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:117
verses.text: Perfectly hath he by this last sentence explained to us all the preceding ones: lest perchance, when he had said, "the Lord looseth them that are fettered," we should refer it to those fettered ones, who for some crime are bound in irons by their masters: and in that he said, "He lifteth up them that are dashed down," there should occur to our minds some one stumbling or falling, or thrown from a horse.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:118
verses.text: There is another kind of fall, there are other kinds of fetters, just as there is other darkness and other light.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:119
verses.text: Whereas he said, "He maketh the blind wise;" he would not say, He enlightened the blind, lest thou shouldest understand this also in reference to the flesh, as the man was enlightened by the Lord, when He anointed his eyes with clay made with spittle, and so healed him: that thou mightest not look for anything of this sort, when He is speaking of spiritual things, he pointeth to a sort of light of wisdom, wherewith the blind are enlightened.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:120
verses.text: Therefore in the same way as the blind are enlightened with the light of wisdom, so are the fettered set free, and those who are dashed down are lifted up.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:121
verses.text: Whereby then have we been fettered? whereby dashed down? Our body was once an ornament to us: now, we have sinned, and thereby have had fetters put on us.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:122
verses.text: What are our fetters? Our mortality.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:123
verses.text: "The Lord loveth the righteous".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:124
verses.text: And who are the "righteous"? How far are they righteous now? Just as thou hast; "the Lord, guardeth proselytes".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:125
verses.text: "Proselytes" are strangers.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:126
verses.text: Every Church of the Gentiles is a stranger.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:127
verses.text: For it cometh in to the Fathers, not sprung of their flesh, but their daughter by imitating them.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:128
verses.text: Yet the Lord, not any man, guardeth them.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:129
verses.text: "The orphan and widow He will take up".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:130
verses.text: Let none think that He taketh up the orphan for his inheritance, or the widow for any business of hers.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:131
verses.text: True, God doth help them; and in all the duties of the human race, he doeth a good work, who taketh care of an orphan, who abandoneth not a widow: but in a certain way we are all orphans, not because our Father is dead, but because He is absent.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:132
verses.text: "And the way of sinners He shall root out".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:133
verses.text: What is, "the way of sinners"? To mock at these things which we say.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:134
verses.text: "Who is an orphan, who a widow? What kingdom of heaven, what punishment of hell is there? These are fables of the Christians.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:135
verses.text: To what I see, to that will I live: "let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:136
verses.text: Beware lest such men persuade you of aught: let them not enter through your ears into your heart; let them find thorns in your ears: let him, who seeketh to enter thus, go away pierced: for "evil communications corrupt good manners".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:137
verses.text: But here perhaps thou wilt say, "Wherefore then are they prosperous? Behold, they worship not God, and commit every kind of evil daily: yet they abound in those things, through want of which I toil".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:138
verses.text: Be not envious against sinners.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:139
verses.text: What they receive, thou seest; what is in store for them, seest thou not?Wilt thou not believe even the Lord thy God, who saith, "Broad and spacious is the way that leadeth to destruction, and many there be that walk by it"?  This "way the Lord will root out".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:140
verses.text: And, when "the way of sinners" has been "rooted out," what remaineth for us? "Come, ye blessed of My father, enjoy the Kingdom;" "The Lord shall reign for ever".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:141
verses.text: "O Sion, thy God" shall reign for ever; surely thy God will not reign without thee.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:142
verses.text: "For generation and generation".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:143
verses.text: He hath said it twice, because he could not say it for ever.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:144
verses.text: And think not that eternity is bounded by finite words.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:145
verses.text: The word eternity consists of four syllables; in itself it is without end.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:146
verses.text: It could not be commended to thee, save thus, "for generation and generation".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 146:147
verses.text: Too little hath he said: if he spoke it all day long, it were too narrow: if he spoke it all his life, must he not at length hold his peace? Love eternity: without end shalt thou reign, if Christ be thine End, with whom thou shalt reign for ever and ever, Amen.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:1
verses.text: Psalm CXLVII.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:2
verses.text: It is said to us, "Praise the Lord".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:3
verses.text: This is said to all nations, not to us alone.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:4
verses.text: And these words, sounded forth through separate places by the Readers, each Church heareth separately; but the one same Voice of God proclaimeth unto all, that we praise Him.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:5
verses.text: And as though we asked wherefore we ought to praise the  Lord, behold what reason he hath brought forward: "Praise the Lord," he saith, "for a Psalm is good".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:6
verses.text: Is this all the reward of them that praise?The "Psalm" is praise of God.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:7
verses.text: This then he saith, "Praise the Lord, for it is good to praise the Lord".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:8
verses.text: Let us not thus pass over the praise of the Lord.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:9
verses.text: It is spoken, and hath passed: it is done, and we are silent: we have praised, and then rested; we have sung, and then rested.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:10
verses.text: We go forth to some business which awaits us, and when other employments have found us, shall the praise of God cease in us ? Not so: thy tongue praiseth but for a while, let thy life ever praise.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:11
verses.text: Thus then "a Psalm is good".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:12
verses.text: For a "Psalm" is a song, not any kind of song, but a song to a psaltery.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:13
verses.text: A psaltery is a kind of instrument of music, like the lyre and the harp, and such kinds of instruments, which were invented for music.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:14
verses.text: He therefore who singeth Psalms, not only singeth with his voice, but with a certain instrument besides, which is called a psaltery, he accompanieth his voice with his hands.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:15
verses.text: Wilt thou then sing a Psalm? Let not thy voice alone sound the praises of God; but let thy works also be in harmony with thy voice.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:16
verses.text: To please then the ear, sing with thy voice; but with thy heart be not  silent, with thy life be not still.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:17
verses.text: Thou devisest no fraud in thy heart: thou singest a Psalm to God.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:18
verses.text: When thou eatest and drinkest, sing a Psalm: not by intermingling sweet sounds suited to the ear, but by eating and drinking moderately, frugally, temperately: for thus saith the Apostle, "whether ye eat or drink, or whatever ye do, do all to the glory of God".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:19
verses.text: If by immoderate voracity thou exceedest the due bounds of nature, and gluttest thyself in excess of wine, however great praises of God thy tongue sound, yet thy life blasphemeth Him.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:20
verses.text: After food and drink thou liest down to sleep: in thy bed neither commit any pollution, nor go beyond the license given by the law of God: let thy marriage bed be kept chaste with thy wife: and if thou desire to beget children, yet let there not be unbridled sensuality of lust: in thy bed give honour to thy wife, for ye are both members of Christ, both made by Him, both renewed by His Blood: so doing thou praisest God, nor will thy praise be altogether silent.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:21
verses.text: What, when sleep has come over thee? Let not an evil conscience rouse thee from rest: so doth the innocence of thy sleep praise God.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:22
verses.text: "Let praises be pleasant to our God".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:23
verses.text: How? If He be praised by our good lives.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:24
verses.text: Hear that then praise will be pleasant to Him.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:25
verses.text: In another place it is said, "Praise is not seemly in the mouth of a sinner".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:26
verses.text: If then in the mouth of a sinner praise is not seemly, neither is it pleasant, for that only is pleasant which is seemly.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:27
verses.text: For praise may be pleasant to a man, when he heareth one praising with neat and clever sentiments, and with a sweet voice; but "let praise be pleasant to our God," whose ears are open not to the mouth, but to the heart; not to the tongue, but to the life of him that praiseth.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:28
verses.text: Who is "our God," that praise should be pleasant to Him? He maketh Himself sweet to us, He commendeth Himself to us; thanks to His condescension.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:29
verses.text: "But God commendeth His love to us""in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:30
verses.text: Let us see whether it be the commendation which the Apostle speaketh of, that Christ died for the sinners and ungodly: "the Lord who buildeth up Jerusalem, and gathereth the dispersions of Israel".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:31
verses.text: For the people of Jerusalem are the people of Israel.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:32
verses.text: It is Jerusalem "eternal in the heavens," whereof the Angels are citizens also.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:33
verses.text: All the citizens then of that city, through "seeing God," rejoice in that great and wide and heavenly city; they gaze upon God Himself.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:34
verses.text: But we are wanderers from that city, driven out by sin, that we should not remain there; weighed down by mortality, that we should not return thither.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:35
verses.text: God looked back on our wandering, and He who "buildeth up Jerusalem," restored the part that had fallen.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:36
verses.text: How restored He the part that had fallen?He sent then to our captive estate His Son as a Redeemer.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:37
verses.text: Take with Thee, said He, a bag, bear therein the price of the captives.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:38
verses.text: For He put on Him our mortal flesh, and therein was the Blood, by the shedding of which we were to be redeemed.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:39
verses.text: With that Blood He "gathered the dispersions of Israel".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:40
verses.text: And if He gathered them that before were dispersed, how must we strive that they be gathered who now are dispersed? If the dispersed have been gathered, that in the Hand of the Builder they might be fashioned into the building, how should they be gathered who through disquiet have fallen from the Hand of the Builder? Behold whom we praise; behold to whom we owe praise all our life long.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:41
verses.text: How doth He gather? What doeth He in order to gather? "Who healeth the bruised in heart".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:42
verses.text: Behold the way in which the dispersions of Israel are gathered, by the healing of the bruised in heart.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:43
verses.text: They who are not of a bruised heart, are not healed.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:44
verses.text: What is to bruise the heart? Let it be known, brethren, let it be done, that ye may be able to be healed.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:45
verses.text: For it is told in many other places of Scripture;"the sacrifice of God is a troubled spirit, a bruised and contrite heart God will not despise".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:46
verses.text: He healeth then the bruised in heart, for He draweth nigh unto them to heal them; as is said in another place, "the Lord is nigh unto them who have bruised their heart".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:47
verses.text: Who are they that have "bruised their heart"? The humble.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:48
verses.text: Who are they that have not "bruised their heart"? The proud.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:49
verses.text: The bruised heart shall be healed, the puffed up heart shall be dashed down.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:50
verses.text: For for this purpose perhaps is it dashed down, that being bruised it may be healed.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:51
verses.text: Let not our heart then, brethren, desire to be set upright, before it be upright.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:52
verses.text: It is ill for that to be uplifted which is not first corrected.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:53
verses.text: What are the means whereby He "bindeth up their bruises"? Just as physicians bind up fractures.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:54
verses.text: For sometimes (observe this, beloved; it is well known to those who have observed it, or have heard it from physicians), sometimes when limbs are sound, but are crooked and distorted, physicians break them in order to set them straight, and make a new wound, because the soundness which was distorted was amiss.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:55
verses.text: What are these means whereby He bindeth? The sacraments of this present life, whereby in the mean time we obtain our comfort: and all the words we speak to you, words which sound and pass away, all that is done in the Church in this present time, are the means whereby "He bindeth up our bruises".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:56
verses.text: For just as, when the limb has become perfectly sound, the physician taketh off the bandage; so in our own city Jerusalem, when we shall have been made equal to the Angels, think ye that we shall receive there, what we have received here? Will it be needful then that the Gospel be read to us, that our faith may abide? or that hands be laid upon us by any Bishop? All these are means of binding up fractures; when we have attained perfect soundness, they will be taken off; but we should never attain it, if they were not bound up.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:57
verses.text: "Who telleth the number of the stars, and calleth them all by their names".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:58
verses.text: What great matter is it for God to "tell the number of the stars"! Men even have endeavoured to do this; whether they have been able to achieve it, is their concern; they would not however attempt it, did they not think that they should achieve it.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:59
verses.text: Let us leave alone what they can do, and how far they have attained; for God I think it no great matter to count all the stars.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:60
verses.text: Or doth He perhaps go over the number, lest He should forget it? Is it any great thing for God to number the stars, by whom "the very hairs of your head are numbered"? The stars are certain lights in the Church comforting our night; all of whom the Apostle saith, "In the midst of a crooked and perverse generation, among whom ye shine as lights in the world, holding the Word of life".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:61
verses.text: These stars God counteth; all who shall reign with Him, all who are to be gathered into the Body of His only-begotten Son, He hath counted, and still counteth them.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:62
verses.text: Whoso is unworthy, is not even counted.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:63
verses.text: Many too have believed, or rather may, with a kind of shadowy appearance of faith, have attached themselves to His people: yet He knoweth what He counteth, what He winnoweth away.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:64
verses.text: For so great is the height of the Gospel, that it hath come to pass as was said, "I have declared, and have spoken: they are multiplied above number:" there are then among the people certain supernumeraries, so to speak.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:65
verses.text: What do I mean by supernumeraries? More than will be there.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:66
verses.text: Within these walls are more than will be in the kingdom of God, in the heavenly Jerusalem; these are above the number.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:67
verses.text: Let each one of you consider whether he shineth in darkness, whether he refuseth to be led astray by the dark iniquity of the world; if he be not led astray, nor conquered, he will be, as it were, a star, which God already numbereth.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:68
verses.text: "And calling them all by their names," he saith.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:69
verses.text: Herein is our whole reward.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:70
verses.text: We may have certain names with God, that God may know our names, this we ought to wish, for this to act, for this to busy ourselves, as far as we are able; not to rejoice in other things, not even in certain spiritual gifts.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:71
verses.text: When the disciples returned from their mission exulting, and saying, "Lord, even the devils are subject unto us in Thy Name" —then He (knowing that many would say, "have we not in Thy Name cast out devils?" to whom He should say, "I know you not") said, "In this rejoice not, that the devils are subject unto you; but rather rejoice, because your names are written in heaven".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:72
verses.text: "Great is our Lord".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:73
verses.text: The Psalmist is filled with joy, he hath poured out his words wonderfully: yet somewhat he was unable to speak, and how availed he to think on it? "And great is His power, and of His understanding is no numbering".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:74
verses.text: He who "numbereth the stars," Himself cannot be numbered.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:75
verses.text: Who can expound this? who can worthily even imagine what is meant by, "and of His understanding is no number"?Whatsoever then that is infinite this world containeth, though it be infinite to man, yet is not to God: too little is it to say, to God: even by the angels it is numbered.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:76
verses.text: His understanding surpasses all calculators; it cannot be counted by us.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:77
verses.text: Numbers themselves who numbereth? What than is there with God? wherewith made He all things, and where made He all things, to whom it is said, "Thou hast arrayed all things in measure, number, and weight"?  Or who can number, or measure, or weigh, measure and number and weight themselves, wherein God hath ordered all things? Therefore, "of His understanding is no number".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:78
verses.text: Let human voices be hushed, human thoughts still: let them not stretch themselves out to incomprehensible things, as though they could comprehend them, but as though they were to partake of them, for partakers we shall be.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:79
verses.text: Partakers then we shall be: let none doubt it: Scripture saith it.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:80
verses.text: And of what shall we be partakers, as though these were parts in God, as though God were divided into parts? Who then can explain how many become partakers of one single substance? Require not then that which I think ye see cannot fitly be said: but return to the healing of the Saviour, bruise your heart.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:81
verses.text: He will guide it, He will bind it up where it is broken, He will make it perfectly sound; and then those things will not be impossible with us, which now are impossible.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:82
verses.text: For it is good that he confess weakness, who desireth to attain to the divine nature.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:83
verses.text: "The Lord taketh up the gentle".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:84
verses.text: For example; thou understandest not, thou failest to understand, canst not attain: honour God's Scripture, honour God's Word, though it be not plain: in reverence wait for understanding.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:85
verses.text: Be not wanton to accuse either the obscurity or seeming contradiction of Scripture.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:86
verses.text: There is nothing in it contradictory: somewhat there is which is obscure, not in order that it may be denied thee, but that it may exercise him that shall afterward receive it.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:87
verses.text: When then it is obscure, that is the Physician's doing, that thou mayest knock.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:88
verses.text: He willed that thou shouldest be exercised in knocking; He willed it, that He might open to thee when thou knockest.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:89
verses.text: By knocking thou shalt be exercised; exercised, thou shalt be enlarged; enlarged, thou shalt contain what is given.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:90
verses.text: Be not then indignant for that it is shut; be mild, be gentle.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:91
verses.text: Kick not against what is dark, nor say, It were better said, if it were said thus.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:92
verses.text: For how canst thou thus say, or judge how it is expedient it be said? It is said as it is expedient it be said.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:93
verses.text: Let not the sick man seek to amend his remedies: the Physician knoweth how to temper them: believe Him who careth for thee.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:94
verses.text: Therefore what cometh next?"The Lord taketh up the gentle, but humbleth the sinners even to the ground," he intended a certain sort of sinners to be understood, from the gentleness mentioned first.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:95
verses.text: By sinners then in this place, we understand the fierce, and those who are not gentle.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:96
verses.text: Wherefore doth He "humble them even to the earth"? They carp at objects of understanding, they shall perceive only things earthly.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:97
verses.text: "Begin to the Lord in confession".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:98
verses.text: Begin with this, if thou wouldest arrive at a clear understanding of the truth.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:99
verses.text: If thou wilt be brought from the road of faith to the profession of the reality, "begin in confession".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:100
verses.text: First accuse thyself: accuse thyself, praise God.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:101
verses.text: What after confession? Let good works follow.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:102
verses.text: "Sing unto our God u pon the harp".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:103
verses.text: What is, "Upon the harp"? As I have already explained, just like the Psalm upon the psaltery, so also is the "harp:" not with voice only, but with works.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:104
verses.text: "Who covereth the heaven with clouds, who prepareth rain for the earth".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:105
verses.text: Now thou art alarmed, because thou canst not see the heaven: when it hath rained thou shalt gather fruit, and shalt see clear sky.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:106
verses.text: Perhaps our God hath done this.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:107
verses.text: For had we not the obscurity of Scripture as an occasion, we should not say to you those things wherein ye rejoice.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:108
verses.text: This then perhaps is the rain whereat ye rejoice.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:109
verses.text: It would not be possible for it to be expressed to you by our tongue, were it not that God covereth with clouds of figures the heaven of the Scriptures.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:110
verses.text: For this purpose willed He that the words of the Prophets should be obscure, that the servants of God might afterwards have that by interpreting which they might flow over the ears and hearts of men, that they might receive from the clouds of God the fatness of spiritual joy.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:111
verses.text: "Who maketh grass to grow upon the mountains, and herb for the service of men".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:112
verses.text: Behold the fruit of the rain.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:113
verses.text: "Who maketh," saith he, "grass to grow upon the mountains".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:114
verses.text: Doth it not also grow upon the low ground? Yes, but it is a great thing that it groweth "on the mountains".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:115
verses.text: For nothing could be more barren than the hard mountains.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:116
verses.text: "And herb for the service of men".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:117
verses.text: What "service"? Listen to Paul himself.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:118
verses.text: "And ourselves," saith he, "your servants for Jesus Christ's sake".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:119
verses.text: He who said, "If we have sown unto you spiritual things, is it a great thing if we reap your carnal things?" yet said, that he was a "servant".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:120
verses.text: For we are your servants, brethren.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:121
verses.text: Let none of us speak of himself, as though he were greater than you.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:122
verses.text: We shall be greater if we are more humble.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:123
verses.text: "But whosoever will be great among you" (it is the Lord's saying), "shall be your servant".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:124
verses.text: Paul the Apostle, indeed, living by his own labour, refused even to receive "the grass of the mountains;" he chose to want; nevertheless, the mountains gave "grass".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:125
verses.text: Because he chose not to receive, ought the mountains therefore not to give, and so to remain barren? Fruit is due to the rain, food is due to the servant, as the Lord saith, "Eat such things as they give you:" and that they should not think that they gave aught of their own, He added, "for the labourer is worthy of his hire".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:126
verses.text: Just now has been read, "Give to every one that asketh of thee;" and in another place Scripture saith, "Let alms sweat in thy hand, till thou findest a righteous man to whom to give it".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:127
verses.text: One there is who seeketh thee, another thou oughtest to seek.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:128
verses.text: Leave not indeed him who seeketh thee empty, for, "give to every one that asketh of thee;" yet still there is another whom thou oughtest to seek; "find a righteous man to whom to give it".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:129
verses.text: Ye will never do this, unless ye have somewhat set aside from your substance, each what pleaseth him according to the needs of his family, as a sort of debt to be paid to the treasury.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:130
verses.text: If Christ have not a state of His own, neither hath He a treasuryCut off then and prune off some fixed sum either from thy yearly profits or thy daily gains, else thou seemest as it were to give of thy capital, and thy hand must needs hesitate, when thou puttest it forth to that which thou hast not vowed.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:131
verses.text: Cut off some part of thy income; a tenth if thou choosest, though that is but little.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:132
verses.text: For it is said that the Pharisees gave a tenth; "I fast twice in the week, I give tithes of all that I possess".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:133
verses.text: And what saith the Lord? "Except your righteousness exceed the righteousness of the Scribes and Pharisees, ye shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:134
verses.text: He whose righteousness thou oughtest to exceed, giveth a tenth: thou givest not even a thousandth.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:135
verses.text: How wilt thou surpass him whom thou matchest not? "Who prepareth rain for the earth".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:136
verses.text: "And giveth unto the cattle their food".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:137
verses.text: These are the cattle he meaneth, even God's flocks.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:138
verses.text: God defraudeth not His flock of their food through men, for whose "service He maketh the grass to grow".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:139
verses.text: "And to the young of the ravens that call upon Him".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:140
verses.text: Shall we perchance think this, that the ravens call upon God to give them their food? Think not that the unreasoning creature calls upon God: no creature knows how to call upon God, save the reasonable alone.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:141
verses.text: Consider it as spoken in a figure, lest thou think, as some evil men say, that the souls of men migrate into cattle, dogs, swine, ravens.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:142
verses.text: Give this no place in your hearts or in your faith.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:143
verses.text: The soul of man is made after the image of God: He will not give His image to dog or swine.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:144
verses.text: Who are "the young of the ravens"? The Israelites used to say that they alone were righteous, because to them the Law had been given: all other men of every nation they used to call sinners.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:145
verses.text: And in truth all nations were given up to sin, to idolatry, to the worship of stones and stocks: but did they continue so? Although the ravens themselves, our fathers, did not, yet we, "the young of the ravens," do call upon GodFor "the young of the ravens," who seemed to worship the images of their forefathers, have advanced, and turned to God.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:146
verses.text: And now thou hearest "the young of the ravens" calling upon the one God.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:147
verses.text: What then? Sayest thou to "the young of the ravens," "hast thou left thy father?" Plainly I have, saith he; for he is a raven who calls not upon God.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:148
verses.text: I, "the young of the raven," do call upon God.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:149
verses.text: "In the power of an horse He will not take pleasure".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:150
verses.text: The power "of an horse" is pride.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:151
verses.text: For the horse seemeth adapted as it were to bear a man aloft, that he may be more uplifted as he goes.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:152
verses.text: And in truth he has a neck which typifieth a sort of pride.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:153
verses.text: Let not men exalt themselves upon their worth, let them not think themselves uplifted by their distinctions; let them beware lest they be thrown by an untamed horse"Nor in the tabernacle of a man will He delight".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:154
verses.text: For the tabernacle of the Lord is the Holy Church spread throughout the whole world.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:155
verses.text: Heretics, separating themselves from the Church's tabernacles, have set up tabernacles for themselves.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:156
verses.text: For if perchance it be the lot of any, who is good and pious, who confesseth his own weakness, who is "the young of a raven that calleth on God," not to enjoy worldly distinction, he goeth not out of the Church, he setteth not up for himself a tent outside the Church, wherein God will not delight.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:157
verses.text: But what saith he? "I have chosen to be cast away in the house of God, rather than to dwell in the tents of sinners".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:158
verses.text: But what addeth he? "The Lord will delight in them that fear Him, and in them that hope in His mercy".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:159
verses.text: A robber is feared, and a wild beast is feared, and an unjust and powerful man is much feared.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:160
verses.text: "The Lord will delight in them that hope in His mercy".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:161
verses.text: Behold, Judas, who betrayed our Lord, feared, but he did not hope in His mercy.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:162
verses.text: It is well indeed that thou hast feared, but only if thou trustedst in His mercy, whom thou hast feared.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:163
verses.text: He in despair "went and hanged himself".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:164
verses.text: In such wise then fear the Lord, that thou trust in His mercy.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:165
verses.text: "Praise in unison, O Jerusalem, thy God".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:166
verses.text: Abiding yet in captivity, they behold those flocks, or rather, the one flock of all its citizens, gathered from all sides into that city; they see the joy of the mass, now after threshings and winnowings placed in the garner, fearing nothing, suffering no toil nor trouble; and, as yet abiding here, in the midst of the threshing they send forward their joy of hope, and pant for it, joining as it were their hearts to the Angels of God, and to that people which shall abide with them in joy for ever.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:167
verses.text: For what wilt thou then do, O Jerusalem? Surely toil and groaning will pass away.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:168
verses.text: What wilt thou do? wilt thou plough, or sow, or plant vines, or make voyages, or trade? What wilt thou do? Will it still be thy duty to be engaged in the works thou now doest, good though they are, and spring from mercy? Consider thy numbers, consider on all sides thy company: see whether any hungers, for thee to give bread to; see whether any thirsts, for thee to give a cup of cold water to; see whether any is a stranger, for thee to take in; see whether any is sick, for thee to visit; see whether any is at strife, for thee to reconcile him; see whether any is dying, for thee to bury him.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:169
verses.text: What then wilt thou do? "Praise in unison, O Jerusalem, thy God".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:170
verses.text: Behold, this is thy business.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:171
verses.text: As is wont to be said in inscriptions, "Use it and be happy".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:172
verses.text: Be ye Jerusalem; remember of whom it is said, "Lord, in Thy city their image Thou shalt bring to nought".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:173
verses.text: These are they who now rejoice in such pomps; among them are they who have not come hither to-day because there is a show.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:174
verses.text: To whom is it a gift? to whom is it a loss? or why is it a gift? why is it a loss? For not they only who exhibit such shows are smitten with loss, but with much greater loss are they smitten who delight in gazing on them.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:175
verses.text: The former have their chest drained of its gold, the latter have their breast robbed of the riches of righteousness.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:176
verses.text: Most of the exhibiters of shows have to mourn for selling their estates; how ought the sinners to mourn, for losing their souls: Was it then for this that the Lord cried out on the Lord's Day, "Watch ye," that to-day men should watch in this way.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:177
verses.text: I beseech you, ye citizens of Jerusalem, I beseech you by the peace of Jerusalem, by the Redeemer, the Builder, the Ruler of Jerusalem, that ye address your prayers to God for them.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:178
verses.text: May they see, may they feel, that they are trifling; and, intent as they are on the sights which please them, may at length look on themselves, and be displeased.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:179
verses.text: For in many we rejoice that this has already been done: and once we too sat there and were mad: and how many think we now sit there, who shall yet be, not only Christians, but also Bishops! From what is past, we conjecture what is to be: from what has already been done, we announce beforehand what God will do.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:180
verses.text: Let your prayers be wakeful, ye groan not for nothing.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:181
verses.text: Certainly they who have already escaped, praying for those who are still in danger, because they too having been among those in danger, are heard; and God shall drag His people out of the captivity of Babylon; by all means He shall redeem and deliver them, and the number of the saints who bear the image of God shall be perfected.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:182
verses.text: "Praise in unison," because thou consistest of many: "praise," because thou hast been made one "We being many," saith the Apostle, "are one in Christ".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:183
verses.text: As then we are many, "we praise in unison;" as we are one, we "praise".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:184
verses.text: The same are many and one, because He in whom they are one is ever One.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:185
verses.text: Wherefore, saith this Jerusalem, do I praise in unison the Lord, and, as Sion, praise my God? Jerusalem is the same as Sion.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:186
verses.text: For different reasons has it the two names.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:187
verses.text: Jerusalem meaneth "visions of peace;" Sion meaneth "watching".

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:188
verses.text: See whether these words do not sound like sights; that the Gentiles may not think that they have sights and we have none.

verses.name: Augustin: Psalms 147:189
verses.text: Sometimes after the theatre or amphitheatre breaks up, when the crowd of lost ones begins to be vomited forth from that den, sometimes, retaining in their minds images of their vain amusements, and feeding their memory with things not only useless but even hurtful, rejoicing in them as if they were sweet, while they are really deadly; they see often, it may be, the servants of God pass by, they recognise them by their garb or headdress, or they know them by sight, and they say to one another, or inwardly, "Wretched people, how much they lose!"
